utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Judge Kamenova has the same problem as caused her absence on Friday afternoon, but we hope that she'll be able to join us later this morning. Meanwhile, we've decided that it is in the interests of justice to continue in her absence. We'll review the position obviously if that absence extends longer than anticipated. The next witness, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, the next prosecution witness is Jose-Pablo Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a mistake in the transcript. Mr. Ojdanic is present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, that's noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: My name is Jose-Pablo Baraybar, doctorum [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Where are you currently employed, Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I am currently employed in the United Nations Mission in Kosovo, UNMIK. I'm the head of the Office of Missing Persons and Forensics, the Department of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Since when have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: June 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Baraybar, that you are a forensic anthropologist by profession?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you very briefly describe your educational background for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Sure. I obtained a first degree in archaeology back in Peru. I did a master's in science at the University of London combining bioarchaeology, physical anthropology, and forensics. I spent a year in the doctoral programme at the University of Champaigne-Urbana in the states, and I shortly ago started my doctorate at the University of Strasbourg in France.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Prior to working for OMPF in Kosovo, where else had you carried out work as a forensic anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I spent a number of years in this Tribunal working for the Office of the Prosecutor as forensic anthropologist. Prior to that, I worked for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda as well, doing the same thing. Prior to that, I worked for the United Nations in Haiti doing the same thing, and before that and in between I also was part of a number of commissions of inquiry in which my expertise was required in other countries in Africa, central America and south America.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your CV --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which is were Your Honours, appendix A to Exhibit 2794 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- contains further details as to your professional background and related activities and I'm not to go through all this document since the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You provided this document to the Office of the Prosecution in October -- your CV in October 2006. Are there any updates or additional information you would like to provide which is not contained in the CV?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The only one I would say is that my office in Kosovo was awarded last November the UN 21 awards for the best field-based project in the UN system. And there are a couple of other publications that are not here but did not really -- did not change the whole CV as it stands at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the UN 21 awards that are given to UN staff members for outstanding achievements in the performance of their duties within the UN, system, is that --

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Baraybar, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in late October/early November 2006 in relation to the mandate and structure of OMPF?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the chance to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Having reviewed your statement, are you satisfied that the information contained in this statement is accurate and true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness statement is Exhibit P2794, and I wish to tender it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you also provide or prepare a report for the Office of the Prosecution in October of last year regarding findings of OMPF forensic inspections on human remains found in three mass grave sites in Serbia after their transfer to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is, Your Honours, appendix C to Exhibit P2794.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in November did you prepare a one-page corrigendum --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm being asked to slow down. I know we're speaking the same language, so we have to pause between question and answer. Mr. Baraybar, in November of 2006 did you provide a corrigendum to your report, specifically to page 11 of your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is P2795, which I seek to tender at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It belongs to one particular point in the -- oh, yeah, page 11 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's page 11 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just a correction to a graph that's on that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I would like to focus on your report of October 2006. Your report concerns three mass grave sites found in Serbia. This would be Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Lake Perucac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand from your report and also from your written statement that prior to the establishment of OMPF in 2002 Serbian forensic teams carried out exhumations and forensic examination on the remains found in these mass graves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When did the transfer or repatriation of the remains found in these mass graves to Kosovo begin to take place?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Between November 2002 and July last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the transfer concluded in July of last year, the transfer of remains back to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand that this repatriation of remains began once DNA analysis established that the persons -- that these remains belonged to individuals who had gone missing during the conflict in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, although the first group of remains transferred in November 2002 were done so without DNA results. DNA results became available after the transfer, not prior to the transfer, as was the case in the other transfers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And OMPF --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please make a pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm reminded again that we have to pause because we're speaking the same language. I'll start my question again. You said that the transfer began in November 2002. Would this be when OMPF took custody of the remains?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. Just to clarify, OMPF was opened in June 2002. In November 2002 we organised the first transfer of remains from Serbia. At the time there were no DNA results as such available for the remains we transferred. After that transfer, the subsequent transfers did have DNA results prior to the transfer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To complete that, are you saying that for the November 2002 transfer, you subsequently got DNA results or did you never get DNA results for those ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did get DNA results after we have transferred the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, if I may, just to complete what I'm trying to explain, because otherwise, it will be left in the air. The November transfer was organised after an exhibition of photographs of clothing that families did identify as belonging to the relatives and based on that, a preliminary identification was carried out and based on that the transfer was arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You explain in your statement how the hand-over takes place in practice and I don't want to deal with that at this stage, because it's sufficiently clear in your statement. Could you explain, what is the purpose of the OMPF forensic inspections which are performed on the remains that are transferred from Serbia proper to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: A forensic inspection is very much a -- or should be as a matter of fact a verification of what we have received, meaning when we receive the body-bags physically at gate 3, the administrative border between Kosovo and Serbia, we cannot certainly carry out an inventory of what is in the bag. We have families, media, officials. It's quite complicated. Therefore, this inventory, if you wish, is carried out when we get to the mortuary where we keep the custody of the remains. So we do have a report from the Serbian authorities saying what they have found and allegedly what is in the bag, and we just try to corroborate. So the inspection was devised in that fashion, although it became something else but it was devised in that fashion. So just to answer to your question, that is a forensic inspection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that you carry out this forensic inspection in the mortuary. Where is this mortuary located?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: At the time the mortuary was located in the -- in the village of Orahovac/Rahovec, in the western part of Kosovo. It's a place where actually ICTY carried out their own operations in the year 2000. Now -- sorry, now it is located in Pristina in a new facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that they were devised in that fashion but they became something else. Could you elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: What I mean by that is that while the objective was to try to corroborate -- just to inspect, to have a look, if you wish, of what was in the bag, at the very beginning it became apparent that there were some contradictions between what was in the bag and what was in the report. For example, in some occasions you could find multiple body parts that belonged to more than one individual in the bag, although the report stated that there was only one person with a name. Obviously, in that situation you could not just simply give the remains back to the alleged family, knowing that they were more than one person and you did not know who the other person was; that was one instance. The second instance was when it became obvious that in some cases we had obvious injuries observed in the remains, and these injuries were not mentioned in the report or if they were mentioned in the report, they were attributed to different mechanisms. For example, just to give you a practical example, a gun-shot wound to the head being attributed to blunt force injury mechanism. And the third instance was that if injuries were recorded, they were not used to ascertain the most probable cause of death in that case we were dealing with. So the inspection became sort of a second autopsy, although with a much more cursory autopsy, if you wish, that was also a second autopsy with a much more in-depth verification, if you wish, of what was contained in that bag.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say that there were some contradictions between what was in the bag and the report, by report you're referring to the reports prepared by the Serbian forensic teams?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct. That is a documentation we received among other documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us who usually takes part in these forensic inspections.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: From our team we had a team of pathologists, anthropologists, identification officers, police officers to take custody of any exhibits that may be still associated to the remains like bullets. Was extremely common to find bullets still with the remains. In some other occasions other artefacts that were maybe forgotten or left by mistake, like knives, I mean, autopsy knives and surgical equipment that came actually from the previous autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you yourself performed any of these forensic inspections or attended any of the forensic inspections when they have been carried out?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. A large number, I would say, I have either participated or been in a sort of supervisory role while they were being carried out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do the forensic inspections conclude with the drafting of a forensic inspection report where the findings are -- of the inspection are indicated?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Once this forensic inspection report is prepared, does OMPF issue a death certificate for the individual whose remains have been inspected?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the cause of death that is contained in that death certificate when one is mentioned, would that be the cause of death that was found during the forensic inspection report?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During the forensic inspection?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the remains that were returned from Serbia from these mass graves, were they for the most part skeletalised remains, that is, remains with very little or no soft tissue on them?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, not all of them. I would say primarily -- if we have three sites, the three sides from which remains were transferred, meaning Batajnica, Perucac, and Petrovo Selo, the first two were primarily skeletalised with very little or no soft tissue or very, very decomposed beyond recognition soft tissue. But in Petrovo Selo they were saponified, primarily saponified, meaning saturation of body fat, so the body looked pretty much like a body, like a cadaver, so there were a striking difference between those two sets of sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is it normally the role of the forensic anthropologist to establish the cause of death during a forensic inspection?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In the case of these remains where you have such a large number of skeletalised remains, does a forensic anthropologist play any role in assisting to establish the cause of death based on the examination of the remains?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: A forensic anthropologist plays a role in both situations, primarily in the reconstruction of broken bones, if I may say it crudely, and also ascertaining the mechanism by which those bones are broken, primarily because forensic anthropologists do work with bones and broken bones. And I understand how bones break, what are the mechanisms behind those. And based on that, it discusses its findings with the pathologist, who certainly has a prerogative to ascertain based on that evidence the most probable cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is the practice of ascertaining the most probable cause of death during this forensic inspection?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It was clearly understood from OMPF standpoint that we would have the duty to use whatever evidence available to us - and I mean objective evidence, recorded evidence - to ascertain the cause of death whenever possible. In other words, if I had in a given autopsy with a pathologist a skeleton, a complete skeleton that has no broken bones, no visible injuries of any kind, the cause of death would definitely be unascertained. Meaning it is not possible to ascertain it based on what I had on the table. However, if you have the same skeleton that has a number of holes in the head that have been defined as being gun-shot wounds to the head based on a number of characteristics, the -- the causative element or phenomena that would have unleashed, if you wish, the process of death would be the gun-shot fired to this individual. Therefore, the cause of death would be found by the pathologist as multiple gun-shot wounds to the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how are you able to distinguish when examining these remains between what would be a gun-shot wound trauma and any other type of trauma that might have been sustained by the individual prior to his death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If I may, I will put it in the simplest of terms, but please, Your Honour, do interrupt me to clarify things. There are major differences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The simpler the better, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try my best. There are major differences between blunt force and gun-shot wound trauma on bone. Blunt force trauma is damage caused over a large area of the bone, primarily by a slow load, meaning a force applied slowly over a large surface. There is some exceptions in which the velocity or the force can be applied much more faster, such as, for example, a car crash in which the body has been accelerated and is impacting against the steering wheel or some part of the car over a large area. As a norm, blunt force is slow-loading, low-velocity. I hit somebody on the head with a hammer. The velocity of the hammer hitting the head would be a few metres per second, so that is slow-loading and a low-velocity. Gun-shot wound trauma is exactly the reverse. It is very high velocity, hundreds of metres per second energy transfers through a very small area. A small area perforates the bone and it dissipates a lot of energy through fracturing. In other words, if somebody is shot in the same head we just hit with a hammer a moment ago, if we just shot it, we will have a hole that is a concentrated energy of the projectile perforating that bone and a lot of fracturing being caused by the energy dispersed, the energy that the projectile contained that passes through the bone and disperses, breaking it in a number of fragments. Is that satisfying, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You're simply confirming what I think I already read in your report, which is helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, how can you distinguish when you're examining these remains between fractures that were caused before or at the time of death and post mortem trauma?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Primarily -- the primary differences you are looking at fractures caused by high velocity or fractures caused by a low velocity. Depending on that and the location of those fractures, you can establish whether these fractures were caused during the peri-mortem, meaning interval around death or after death. For example, transverse fractures of long bones, meaning severed members, have been seen and examined by us during our work as a matter of fact over the years. For the Srebrenica case in which a number of bodies were placed in mass graves and then removed from those graves to secondary graves, causing a lot of damage by the excavators, so this is a very classical example of post mortem fracturing, transverse fractures of long bones. That is one characteristic. Another characteristic is crushing of body parts with plastic deformation, meaning let's take as an example this plastic pen here. If I bend it, I may bend it a bit and the plastic will yield and deform, but if I try to put it back to its original shape, I won't be able to. That's a plastic deformation. Bones do deform in that way as well. That is equivalent to a slow load, most likely crushing from the pressure of the earth on the grave and things of the kind; while other type of fracturing, such as that caused by bullets, for example, might break a bone in a number of pieces, but you can easily reconstruct it together and then see the -- the specific damage that was caused to it, for example, by a bullet, you will see the bullet-hole in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have now Exhibit P2795 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is the corrigendum that you prepared to the graph on page 11 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could focus on the graph that's there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you very briefly explain what is depicted in this graph on this page 11 or the corrected page 11 of your report.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: This graph shows you -- this graph shows you the cases that were received by OMPF and were examined by OMPF and had been previously examined by the Serbian authorities. We have been indicating in this graph -- or I, rather, have indicated in this graph the number of cases for which cause of death was ascertained and the number of cases for which cause of death was unascertained. So on the first column of 744 to your left, that is a number of cases examined by OMPF when we received them, of which we were able to determine or ascertain cause of death in 508 cases, and then in 238 cases we were not able to ascertain cause of death. And then the same calculation continues for the two other sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just for the sake of clarity, at the bottom of this graph you have a BA, that would stand for Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the B, Lake Perucac?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: P for Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your report on page 10 you have also done a summary of the findings of the Serbian forensic reports or forensic exhumation reports. How do these findings by OMPF compare to the previous findings of the Serbian forensic teams?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, when we received the remains from Batajnica, we noticed that for the 744 cases we report in page 11 on the corrigenda on page 11, cause of death had been unascertained for the whole of 744 cases in the case of Batajnica. The same thing for the site D, as Lake Perucac. However, in Petrovo Selo cause of death had been ascertained for 32 cases. So what you see in the corrigenda on page 11 is very much the difference between the ascertainment of cause of death after the forensic inspection. So if 744 cases in the first autopsy were not -- did not yield a cause of death, after forensic inspection 506 of those cases did yield a cause of death, so it's roughly 66 per cent of the cases did yield a cause of death and so on in the other site.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have page 34 of Exhibit P2794 up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is page 11 of your report. You provide in your report three examples where you compare the findings of the Serbian forensic teams with the findings of the OMPF forensic inspections, and I would like to concentrate on this first case Ba-12 which is on page 11 or page 34 of this exhibit in e-court. If you will notice, it's already up on your screen.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you just wait. I don't have it up here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we focus on the bottom half of the page, if we could zoom in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In the code here Ba-12 that is referred to in this case, it would be the code that was given by the Serbian forensic teams?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you kept the same code for the forensic inspection reports and later in the death certificates for this individual. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain looking here at the photographs that we have on the screen how the OMPF forensic team was able to establish the cause of death for this individual.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly. What we see on page 11 at the bottom on these three shots are three different views of a skull, of a human skull, that show a large cavity on the top of the skull and some erosion of the bone and some blackening of the bone around it. This was caused by fire, not by any gun-shot. This is burning of the bone, of the remains; however, if we go to the next page, on page number 12 of my report --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe it's in the report.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: On the picture on the right you can see this elongated defect, hole, if we use a more popular term, that is what we will define as a keyhole injury, that is a gun-shot injury that hits the skull in a tangential fashion that has two elements combining an entrance and an exit at the same time. Upon review of this photograph I have a minor disagreement with the anthropologist who examined this case regarding the direction of the shot. In the report it is stated that it is from above to below; however, at least on the picture, I would say that it is above to below on the picture, that would be below to above on the person. If you -- how can I point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There is a pen at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If the usher could please assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- At this side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Technology always helps. Thank you. If you see this element here, that little round -- you may see on the left side a little round edge, that would be the entrance component of the defect, and if you see in this area here, you see a slight bevelling of the -- of the edges, that would be the exit component there. This fracture here would be the entrance fracture, and this fracture here and there, like a Y, like an inverted Y, would be the exit fractures that are associated to this bevelling. So this is a tangential gun-shot wound to the head, also known as a keyhole. Such injury would be the one causing death to the person, as defined by the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, this type of fracture would be characteristic of a gun-shot wound?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we move now to page 38 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is page 15 of the report. On this page you have presented a graph where you show the distribution of injuries per anatomical area. I don't know if it's already up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain what is depicted here on this graph and tell us which conclusions, if any, can be drawn from this pattern of injury.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, as you see here we discuss the minimal number of gun-shot injuries. This means that one -- not every individual was shot once. Many people showed gun-shot wounds to the head and trunk and limbs and -- or just simply on the head or simply on the trunk, so therefore, it is the minimal number. So at least 300 people were shot in the head, at least 323 on the trunk, but certainly some of the people were shot on the trunk were also shot on the head and vice versa. Now, there's a number of conclusions that can be drawn from this. The first one is that the number of people who did not sustain gun-shot injuries but that sustained shrapnel injuries was very, very low, meaning four, to be more precise. As a matter of fact, three of them, if I've not mistaken, combined both and only one had shrapnel alone without - and I'm looking on my notes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe it's the other way around from what is up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Right. So let me just see here. It shows -- certainly. So three individuals sustained shrapnel and one both. That's what I'm saying. Fine. So all in all, four people sustained shrapnel of some kind in combination or not. Now, what is extremely strange. Now, why would I say "strange?" According to available information on war epidemiology, if we wish to call it this way, meaning how many people are wounded or killed by certain kinds of ammunition in more than combat or non-combat situations, being Afghanistan in the gulf, in the Balkans, or whatever else, the interesting pattern that emerges is the following. In combat situations most of the killed or wounded are done so by fragmenting ammunition, meaning by shrapnel, while the number of people killed or injured by fire-arms is much less. So, for example, we have a quote here from a study done in 1999 in Afghanistan and we've got 73 per cent of the people were killed or wounded by fragmenting ammunition, while 26 per cent by bullets, by fire-arms. These are combat situations. If we go to a non-combat-situation, using a quote in the same study, we have the reverse. The number of people killed/wounded by fragmented ammunition is 30 per cent, while those by fire-arms is 65 per cent. So that is a first situation we have to take into account, and now we can go to this graph. In combat situations, again using other studies, if we look at the people either killed or injured by fire-arms, in a combat situation, people that are wearing full military gear will show injuries in areas unprotected by -- by body armour, meaning the neck, the face, the groin. But in non-combat situations where people obviously are not wearing on them every day body armour, most of injuries caused by, for example, fragmenting ammunition would be in the extremities, in the limbs. The data for fire-arm injuries or the distribution of fire-arm injuries varies. It's very variable. However, in this situation - and we refer to the graph in page number 15 - we see that the highest number of injuries is located in the trunk, followed by the head, and then trailed by a third, by really a third of the total by the limbs. So it is a very strange, to say the least, distribution of gun-shot injuries, primarily because - referring again to these studies - fire-arms, unlike fragmenting ammunition, are what we would call weapons of volition. You are not -- when you throw a mortar, a shell, or whatever, you are not aiming at a person, you are aiming at something, at a target. When you are firing a fire-arm, you are obviously aiming at somebody. You're not firing to the air or to -- or whatever. You're trying to hit somebody. Therefore, these numbers should be taken into that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can any conclusions be drawn as to the circumstances that these individuals whose remains you examined met their deaths?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The opinion -- the opinion I have stated in this report, based again on the sources I have been quoting, is that these injuries represent a way inflicted, rather, on a population unable to defend itself, meaning in a non-combat situation. This is not the type of injuries you would expect to find in a combat situation, but exactly in the opposite. In other words, the ones receiving or sustaining these injuries are not combatants, not by condition, but they're not, let's say, participating in a combat action as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what would be the type of injuries you would expect to find in a combat situation?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: First of all, shrapnel. I mean, as the leading -- the leading type of injury, we should have found is shrapnel; there's exactly the reverse, and not fire-arms. What we said is we have only -- I mean, some 0.6 per cent of shrapnel injuries based on a universe of 889 cases. So we have the reverse pattern to begin with. We have then fire-arms, and then we have an abnormal location of fire-arm injuries among the ones that showed those injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These findings that we're seeing here on this page that you have summarised on this graph refer to Batajnica and Perucac mass grave sites. Do the same conclusions apply for Petrovo Selo, the findings for Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In Petrovo Selo as a matter of fact, it is the same, yes. I mean, the same pattern applies to all sites, no matter -- I mean, no matter how we look at it, 40 individuals showing some kind of shrapnel injuries over 889 is quite substantial in terms of proportions. It's 0.6 per cent of the total has shrapnel in three sites, all the three sites combined.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly from your report for Petrovo Selo, there were no individuals whose remains you examined that had any type of shrapnel injury?

utterances.speaker: JOSE-PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct. And if I may add an important detail, now that you raise Petrovo Selo, that's very important. One could argue, and it's a valid argument, that the skeleton, because it lacks soft tissues, gives you only a fraction of the injuries sustained by the individual, what is true. For example, somebody shot in the abdomen, the bullet comes through and through the abdomen and doesn't touch any bone. When you have the skeleton, you would not know this person was shot; it is completely fair to say that. However, in Petrovo Selo, unlike the other two sites, these were cadavers; they were fully fleshed. And in those fully fleshed cadavers that have a total of -- I don't have the total with me here --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think it's on the next page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we go to page 39.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes, that is the distribution of injuries in Petrovo Selo, but I was looking for the absolute number of 61 cases. On the 61 cases of Petrovo Selo, there's still, I mean, 7 -- roughly 7 per cent of the total of all the cases examined here that were fully fleshed. In none of those cases we recovered shrapnel injuries; again, only gun-shot injuries. So what I'm trying to say is that even if we argue that shrapnel may be lost because they were skeletons and it was not recovered or whatever, and there were a much, much larger proportion of people that suffered shrapnel injuries instead of gun-shot injuries, that would not, I mean, fit. Still we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: General, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE

utterances.text: Now, General, do you have -- you don't have a copy of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So if I could give you a copy.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Things went a bit quicker for me as well this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the statement has been uploaded into e-court as Exhibit number P2772. And at this stage I should mention that what has been uploaded is the witness statement plus all the attachments to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what we'll do is suspend any decision on the admission of all this documentation until we get to a stage in the evidence where we can make a final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was only in light of this objection that I thought I should make clear what the exhibit actually includes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 22, after the second sentence, after the reference to an attachment MM/6, am I correct that you also handed over a second set of minutes of a meeting that you had with Delic on the 1st of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And that is the attachment that's actually referred to in the subsequent paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then on the next page of the statement, paragraphs 28 and 29, I believe there are two other mistakes. Am I correct that the reference to the attachment M6A should actually have been M6B?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 29 the reference to attachment MM/8 should have been MM/7?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Apart from these -- once these corrections are made to your statement, does the statement accurately reflects, as our rules say, your declaration and what you would say today if examined on the issues covered by the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I will seek to tender this statement but not the attachments. Maybe that would be the best way to do it and then we will sort out the attachments afterwards. Or should we simply -- sorry, I don't want to confuse matters. Is it better that I propose to tender the statement but we will get back to this later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, you already mentioned that you testified in the Milosevic case. I believe that was on the 29th and 30th of May, 2002?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review the transcript of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And does that, again, reflect what you would declare and say if you were asked about the same events today?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So -- in due course I will seek to tender this -- these transcripts, and for the record, they have exhibit number in e-court P2815.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 9 of your statement you mention that you on one occasion had a meeting with Mr. Sainovic. And you say in your statement that you had no doubt that he was well-apprised of what was happening in Kosovo. What made you think that? What gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I found certainly Mr. Sainovic -- especially since I had the chance of -- it was Ambassador Keller who was actually running -- leading the meeting, so I had to chance to just sit back and watch his behaviour and I thought he was a confident, polished gentleman, who seemed very well-aware of the activities that were going on in Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you also say that he had the power -- the power to act was in his hands to a great degree. How did --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, my sense was that on other occasions I had been -- obviously in several meetings with all the folks in Kosovo, and there were times when people referred -- would refer to higher authority or would -- would not be able to make decisions immediately. And in this case I don't believe -- certainly from my recollection, I do not remember any instance of Mr. Sainovic saying: "Well, I have to refer this back to my authorities or I'm not in a position to agree or disagree a certain issue or decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as -- the hope is that the Court will have your statement and transcript before them. I'll jump around in your material a little bit just to add some value to the evidence that will already be before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So I would like if we can call up exhibit P2772, which is the statement, and go to page 20 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph number? Is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is one of these attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's attachment M/2A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Called "Guidance for the Conduct of Operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, do you have it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: On the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: In fact, what this is is -- on my arrival on the middle of December to the regional centre in Prizren, there were no -- there were no instructions to my subordinates on how to conduct themselves in the mission. You know, as you know, this mission was set up very quickly and I felt that there was a requirement to issue some orders and some, if you wish, rules for the -- for the behaviour of my people in the regional centre. And so that is the -- that's the document that I issued as the head of the regional centre. I developed it with my subordinates using some of the -- as well some of the experience of the UK KDOM on which my regional centre was based and which absorbed the UK KDOM on start-up of the mission. So these were, if you wish, orders or certainly guidance and direction on my behalf as the head of the regional centre to my subordinates for their behaviour and actions in the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was this document given out to the verifiers that came and worked in your regional centre?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It was given actually to the entire chain of command and with certainly direction that this was to be passed to every one of the verifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In addition to receiving this document, was any kind of training given to verifiers that worked for the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, every verifier that came into the KVM would receive a course at the KVM induction centre in Brezovica, that was run by the Italians actually at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about paragraph 3 of this -- of this document. Could you explain to us what is it you are describing under the heading "Other Forces."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, in the usually NATO format for orders and guidance, there's a paragraph that talks about other forces that may be around in the area of operations. In this case, I -- I divided up into those that are within the Kosovo theatre and those that were outside, and of course NATO had the mission of providing support if there was a requirement to evacuate, and so there were forces outside of Kosovo that were of interest to us, and that's -- that was -- the aim was to describe those forces in paragraph B, 3B, and the fact that these would be coordinated through the Kosovo verification coordination centre in Skopije.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just to make clear, when there's a reference to certain circumstances, what were they, were they evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like if we could move on to paragraph 22 of this exhibit which is in e-court at page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is it more helpful to the court staff if I give the -- our ERN number, the longer number that begins with a K for you to find the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For me it's easiest if I'm given the number in the MM series that you have, since that's how it's been numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We're within the same document. We're still in MM/2A, but now we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are paragraph numbers, so you can give us the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And obviously -- I think we're having another page there, aren't we. We need to go backwards a number -- a couple of pages, six pages I think. The court staff have the right ERN number up at the top. Oh, sorry, we need to go to page 23. I think we're at page 29. Good. Thank you. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, here in paragraph 22 you talk about daily sitreps being prepared by your regional centre. Who approved the sitreps before they were sent off?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I had taken the -- in fact, the sitrep was developed by the chief of operations, who would gather the -- and collate the information from the subordinate coordination centres, and I had taken the habit, as I believe is important, as the commander, as the head of the regional centre to review the sitrep every day and to add my own comments where pertinent on the overall situation, as I believe that the head of a regional centre has perhaps a better overall view and a strategic picture of what's going on in the other areas as well. So essentially, I would write that comment, would review the sitrep, make sure that it was accurate as far as I was -- as I knew. Obviously, I didn't know every detail, but I would certainly try to get as much as I could. And then if I was not there my -- the deputy would do it, and if he wasn't there, then obviously the chief of operations would do it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I will -- I would like to ask you about paragraph 23. Here you set out the approach to be adopted by your verifiers when they are in the field. Now, I will talk about -- you mentioned that this document was prepared by you for your regional centre. Were these kind of principles adopted by other region stall centres, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I certainly was of the hope that they would be, and my -- because, of course, this direction, which -- if things had been in the perfect world would have come from above, from the KVM headquarters down to the regional centres. They had not had a chance to actually sit down and do this kind of document. So I actually produced it and gave a copy to the other regional centres and I passed a copy up to the -- of course, up to KVM headquarters. I don't believe that I saw anywhere a -- you know, as detailed a document from the KVM, although these principles were ones that I elaborated with my -- with my folks, of course, in the mind of the way the KVM was approaching the mission itself, i.e., General DZ and Ambassador Walker wished to behave with impartiality to all parties, unity of effort, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on two pages ahead again in this exhibit. We're now moving to an attachment which is numbered MM/2B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, do you have it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I was -- well, in the military, of course, we try to be ahead of whatever's going to happen next. And at the time of the Rambouillet negotiations, there was a -- we hoped that it was going to yield a positive outcome and to be prepared for that opportunity or that eventuality I sat down with my folks and looked at how we might implement a future accord. And so what this is a kind of a leaning-forward document that talked about the -- in the event of a successful negotiation in Rambouillet, that we would be prepared to implement some measures in terms of, you know, the future of Kosovo itself. And certainly within -- within the regional centre trying to identify areas where we might put folks in what we called shadow positions, liaison positions, those were primarily the areas that we thought would be the first thing that would required if there was an agreement. These liaison and shadow folks would be there as -- if you wish, to keep very close connection with the parties, all the parties and be able to certainly offer an information system for the international community to see how the implementation of the accord would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain to us the difference between a liaison officer and a shadow person?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I guess they're closely -- you could almost say they're almost the same thing where a liaison officer would perhaps be more to an organisation and a shadow person would be more to an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, General, this document is dated on the 23rd of February, so this is towards the end of the Rambouillet negotiations. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you have op success, does that mean operation success?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Operation success. For obvious reasons, we were hoping it would be successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But what were -- did you have an operation or is this a reference to this particular process of preparing and --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: This was a reference to the -- you know, we called it operations success because we thought it might be successful. No more smart than that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, General, the next document I'd like to have a look at is a document that's found still in the same exhibit at page -- e-court page 47. And it is attachment MM/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I guess it's probably one of the documents that my learned friend has an objection to. I haven't looked at the file yet, but I see he's on his feet. If it is, I will not be seeking to tender this document, but there's a reference to it in the Milosevic transcript and therefore I just want to clarify two points about this, so maybe I should just quit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've played all your cards in advance, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You know how we are from the side of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is indeed one of the documents that my Defence team had an objection to that is not contained in the motion. That is the one that I was going to have a short oral submission on. If it's not coming in, I just want to make sure that, although it's referenced in the Milosevic transcript, it's not coming in through the backdoor, either, because I believe this document would be a violation of Rule 92 bis and ter insofar as it's a statement of a non-declarant who's not in court, not under oath, et cetera, and is a purely personal document rather than a business document, which is perhaps the reason why it's not being tendered. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your position then, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If none of my colleagues are going to rely on this document, I don't have any questions about the document. That's my position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, but if I need to, I would tender it, but with two questions about each one of the -- the nature of the two parts of this document only. We will not be relying on the content of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection taken is that it's a device to get around the requirements of Rule 92 ter to produce this document in this way. Do you accept or contest that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I mean we can get into a whole legal issue whether we can tender hearsay evidence and stuff like that. My position on the use of this document for the Prosecution's case is, we're not going to rely on the contents of this document to prove any matters in the Prosecution case. So there isn't a real issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why are you tendering it, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's because -- well, it is because we are seeking to have this transcript from the Milosevic case admitted to where there is a reference to this, so it's going to come in with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it used in cross-examination or examination-in-chief in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's used in cross-examination for a limited purpose, and anticipating that the Defence might want to rely on the document in due course, or some of the accused, I had two questions about the document only to put to the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, do you have a separate point to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Perhaps we can wait for these questions, Your Honour, might answer what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic's objection is to the document per say, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we have to make a ruling here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I certainly don't rely on the document, as Mr. Marcussen said, if any of the Defence lawyers rely on it. We do not rely on the document, but the witness has said that he believes -- he believes that the document's an accurate assessment of what was going on in Kosovo at the time. And I had one or two very brief questions that I had planned to ask him about that document, but again, we do not rely on the document. It is one person's opinion, but to the extent that the general said he agreed with the assessment contained therein, I had one or two very brief questions to ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's something he said in the Milosevic trial, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's actually something he said right in his statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. You maintain your position then, Mr. Ivetic, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think in view of the position we've taken so far on this, we'll ask the two questions to be asked under reservation and we'll make a decision on this along with the others. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, this is a document that has two parts. The first part is a document that was updated on the 27th of December, 1998, which -- you have the first page of the document on your screen before you. Was this document distributed to verifiers in the same way as the -- your guide-line was distributed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, this was more of a -- had more of a restricted distribution, but it was available to the chain of command and I would not say that every verifier read it. But it was available to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to e-court page -- e-court page 62, please. There we have the second part of this attachment to your statement, but it's a separate document also prepared by Mr. Wilson dated the 6th of February, 1999. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Again, this is a -- more of a leaning-forward document. And again, you have to remember these two documents were prepared by an individual and were, you know, his personal view of what was going on. And the second one called "Intervention Forces in Kosovo," to which you refer now is one that was prepared at the outset of the Rambouillet Accords or the Rambouillet discussions and negotiations, and again talks about the possible requirement for an intervention or an implementation force in Kosovo should there be an accord, an agreement, in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And am I understanding you correctly that this is a document that described what the KVM's role would be if such an intervention force was agreed on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I guess that ended up being three questions, but I'll move off the exhibit now. Now, General, moving to sort of a broader topic, the KLA. How would you describe the KLA force during the time you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I guess I would describe it as not a -- not particularly well-organised; nevertheless, having a semblance of a chain of command. A group of folks, I guess, with what they perceived as good intentions, so-called freedom fighters, I guess you could call them and -- but that wished to be taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to assess their strategy and tactics?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, the -- certainly, the one thing that -- in certainly my dealing with them they -- they seemed -- and I was dealing with one particular individual most of the time, that they -- who kept telling me that they had an overall strategy and that they were preparing activities and so on. So it seemed that certainly from what he was saying, they had -- they had an agreed strategy and seemed to be coordinated. Now, that -- you know, that's -- didn't prove to be the case on several occasions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was that individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Drini, his nom de guerre was Drini, that was the individual with whom I negotiated most of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is it possible for you to describe sort of the capabilities that the KLA had in your view as a --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say they were a very, very lightly equipped, usually small-arms, perhaps some machine-guns but no heavy vehicles, no armour, certainly, you know, transported in soft-skinned vehicles, trucks, buses, mini-buses, and so not certainly a military force as you would -- you would find in organised -- you know, in a country, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In this case we have been using sort of a range of various terms that I'd like to ask you about, based on your experience as a senior officer. Could you describe to us your understanding between the distinction between terrorists, guerillas, militaries, and maybe paramilitaries, too, to try to cover the whole set of terms that's been used here?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, if I start off with what certainly I see as a terrorist, as an officer, as a military professional officer, a terrorist to me is not necessarily an organised group of people who are waging war against an enemy other than by using -- using events and activities that make a big splash for media purposes. That would be I guess to the left-hand of the scale. You could call it a -- maybe a political movement or a -- a -- sometimes I guess religious movement as well. On the right-hand side, military forces structured with uniforms and with a hierarchy and a chain of command from the top to the bottom with, perhaps, a political authority or -- yeah, a political authority of some kind at the top. And that's the right-hand of the scale. In the middle I guess you could look at perhaps guerillas as people who organise themselves in a kind of an uprising and are looking to change -- to change a particular situation in kind of a well-meaning freedom kind of desire. So it's -- it's kind of a -- it's not absolute, of course, but I guess in my simple military mind that's the way I divide them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- the term "paramilitary," what does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, paramilitary I guess would be forces that had not -- that are not fully military and designed and organised to go and fight against opposing militaries. Paramilitary would be forces that have perhaps hierarchy and a chain of command and some military skills but not all of them but that are more designed to support civilian action, I guess. Much as a gendarmerie, for example, in some countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that be like the ISS in France, if you're familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, the gendarme, I guess is what you're talking about yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 12 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, we have been having the term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because it could lead to an interminable debate here. Do you have a specific purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do have a specific purpose. There have been already a fair amount of debate about what witnesses have meant when they have referred to paramilitaries, what it means when a statement says paramilitary and things like that. I think the Defence have suggested that that means random people running around on the ground, so I'm asking what in a military -- senior military officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't really matter what the senior military officer thinks a paramilitary is; it depends what the witness who used the expression thought the paramilitary was, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's something we alone can judge since we alone have heard all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So I just wouldn't like us to get into a debate on this subject which does nothing but increase tension rather than help to resolve problems in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But it is a fairly important point for the Prosecution whether, for example, armed units -- the civilians that have been armed by the authorities of the FRY and Serbia qualify as a paramilitary organisation. It's a legal -- now I'm getting into a legal debate, but there is an issue about the classification of some of these different armed groupings that were around in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yes, I understand that and if Mr. Maisonneuve had the personal experience of groupings that fell into the category you have described, then it would be good to hear his evidence but not his general views on how you define terrorists, guerillas, and paramilitary. That, I don't think is going to assist us here. Anyway, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 12 of your statement you -- you say that the military hardware and equipment went beyond bounds of any reasonable anti-terrorist action. And you make reference to similar sort of things in paragraph 18, 35, and 36 of your statement. Now, what equipment did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, in my experience as an army officer and as an armoured officer, a tanker, the approach to -- you try as much as possible to match the threat with the equipment and the approach that you're going to take. For example, tanks and heavy vehicles and motorised -- mechanised forces would be used in open conflict against other tanks in fairly open -- open ground in manoeuvre warfare, if you wish. If you're fighting against a lightly armed force, most likely you would try to match that by lightly armed and perhaps special forces in countering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There's mention in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could you find a suitable point to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let's simply take it here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Maisonneuve, we have to break at this stage, and that break will be for half an hour. Could you please go with the usher; he'll show you where to wait meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marcussen, have you had a chance now to consider the terms of this notice to exclude testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you some questions about it. So far as the transcript is concerned, the reference to pages 5855 to 5892 and 5903 to 5909 are to cross-examination. Do you insist on these pages being part of the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There are a few points that are actually clarified in those passages, but as they are covered also in the direct so it's not -- there are little bits that I would have liked in but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you identify them --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you identify them, we'll consider them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you like me to address the motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that can be done just now, yes. If that is the position, let's do the whole thing in order, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 5768 is neither here nor there, so we'll exclude it. 5778 to 5805, what do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In my submission, this is relevant to -- it is relevant to the linkage -- there -- basically with all of this evidence there are two main points. The first point is that the Prosecution is alleging that there was a general campaign in Kosovo where -- during which a number of instances occurred where excessive force was used. This is one of them, Racak is one of them, so to that extent we are seeking to have the evidence in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know we've made a decision about that. We can't re-visit that decision here, so end of story. We are not investigating Racak. You haven't asked us to review that and we're not doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Evidence has been allowed in through other witnesses - let me address the point - about the kind of forces that were involved, about the chain of command, those kind of issues. They are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example of the evidence of the kind of forces involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, what this evidence is showing in parts of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, in the past. What evidence have we admitted about the kinds of forces involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We've had, for example, General Drewienkiewicz talking about whether or not there was VJ forces on the rim up above Racak village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. And we have had -- so these kind of things are covered by this witness as saying that observers -- KVM observers on the ground on the 15th were with the tank units on the rim and that he was -- he was informed by these people that a house -- a tank fired at a house in Racak village. Now, I'm fully aware that we're not -- I'm not trying to get into the underlying crime base evidence where this is relevant to the cases, the level of coordination that this witness say was required in order for something like this to happen. He's basically saying: If you have police and army operating in this kind of fashion, in his view the coordination would have taken place at least at the brigade and MUP staff level. So that's why I'm seeking to rely on this. This part of the transcript also includes discussions of some of these exhibits that are also objected to such as MM/7 and MM/8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's deal with one thing at a time. We're looking at the transcript. Now, where is it you say in these passages we find something about the level of coordination required for something like this to happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not able to take you to every single -- what I've down is outlined the points that arise from these general chunks of transcript. I have two small points that I thought the Defence would be objecting to that I was going to agree to exclude, but obviously much smaller parts than what the Defence is seeking to have excluded. We have -- there's also a passage in this -- in this evidence about -- generally about MUP conduct in Kosovo. The witness is saying that the MUP was acting, they are overreaching --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's in page four -- 5794 and that sort of thing may well be admissible. There's another passage on 5782 about the use of heavy armaments in circumstances which don't merit it, and these are general expressions of his view as a person who can express such a view. There are passages you can clearly justify having admitted in this area, and we need your guidance on it. You seem to want to go further than would fall into that -- into these categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If Your Honours would like me to address the specific points with specific page references within these hundred pages that are there, I'm not in a position to do that at this stage. In that case I would like to seek leave to file a written submission identifying the specific areas where these points arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think -- I think somebody can surely do that in the course of the day today and we can hear your oral submissions and get this dealt with today. We're not going to build up a backlog of written determinations that remain outstanding. We're getting too close to the end of this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I must say, I do feel a bit ambushed by my learned colleagues on the other side, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This was entirely predictable, Mr. Marcussen, entirely predictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, there's another part of this objection which -- for example, pages 5821, lines 17 through 23, the issue addressed there is whether or not the commander of combat teams, the combat teams that were up on the rim above Racak, was cooperating with the KVM or not. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's not the part that's objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. 5821, lines 17 through 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does that say about being on the rim?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No. What this is saying is this is -- this goes to the issue of whether or not the VJ was cooperating with the KVM. And the witness is saying, whereas the brigade commander that he was -- Delic, that he was normally dealing with was accepting to have meetings with him when there were issues they could discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may well be admissible, but it's got nothing to do with whether they're up on the rim, which is how you introduced this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I moved on. I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not what the transcript reflects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think the problem is with the big chunks that the Defence is seeking to get excluded, there are a lot of different issues arising from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll allow you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- from those specific parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
