utterances.text: We'll allow you to address us later on the specific parts you think should be saved from the transcript, and somebody hopefully can be working on that while you're dealing with the examination. And you will, I expect, have a break at lunchtime when you can look yourself at some of this. So far as the exhibits are concerned, you said that some of these --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, these exhibits -- Exhibit MM/7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, just before you go to that. There's paragraphs from the statement and one of them -- paragraph 36 seemed okay to me. I'm speaking off the cuff at the moment. The others possibly fall within the objection. And then MM/7 was the first of the documents. Has MM/7 been exhibited already?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Even with Colonel Kotur, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I could be mistaken, but I don't think it is. But we will check on that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, why did you say it was admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, do you want me to address the paragraph in the statement or the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, forget the statement. Move to these exhibits because we need to know how to control the rest of the examination and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: MM/7, in my submission, is relevant because it, again, addresses the issue of VJ involvement in Racak. Jelic, in this exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's your basis. What about number 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Number 8, it, again, is the same issue. It confirms -- yet another confirmation by another officer that the VJ was involved in Racak. Number 13, again we have Jelic saying that his headquarters had given the order to the operation. He's, again, confirming VJ involvement. And 13A and 13B essentially all go to the same issue about the VJ being involved. These are -- these are records of meetings with different MUP and VJ officers, recordings of their different answers to, well, a number of questions but including questions about whether or not the VJ was involved, whether tanks were involved. In our submission, all these documents show that the VJ was, indeed, involved in this operation, which, in my submission, as I said, go to the issue of the level of coordination in the operation, which ultimately is one of these linkage points that we are trying to concentrate on in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that is helpful at this stage to have explored these areas. There obviously is a difficult line to draw between what's admissible in relation to demonstrating the command structure and coordination between the VJ and MUP in general, and indeed on the day of the 15th of January, and the detail of the event itself. What is clear, as we're not exploring the detail of the event itself - so there needs to be no cross-examination of documents on material in relation to that - and we will in fact go through the documents to which objection has been taken and we'll excise portions, if necessary, if that is necessary, to make it absolutely clear what is being considered and what is not being considered. And we will be guided to some extent by what we have done previously in the case in relation to this area so that there's consistency in our approach. We will expect the Prosecution to address us further before we finalise this exercise, hopefully first thing this afternoon, and we'll give the Defence an opportunity to respond at that time, if it's necessary to respond in light of the indications we're giving anyway. It should be clear to you that we see force in significant parts of this submission and debate -- and that some parts are debatable. So we shall now return to the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Maisonneuve. We have been trying to at least resolve in part the issues that are outstanding as legal matters for us. They're not entirely resolved and there might be another interruption to your evidence for that purpose, but meanwhile we shall proceed to hear more of your own evidence. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, we took off at a point where you were describing various kinds of military equipment and how that kind of heavier equipment would normally be used. Now, there's reference ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Marcussen. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is reference in parts of your evidence to a howitzer. What kind of a weapon is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: To which, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: A howitzer.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Howitzer.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Howitzer, yes. Those are artillery weapons of different calibres and they are usually used in the indirect role; that is, you know, they'll be behind a hill and they'll fire over a hill to support their artillery pieces that support infantry on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what kind of an effect would these kind of weapons have if you shoot at a normal house, dwelling? A house can be different in nature, but are you able to assist on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, certainly, they have different types of ammunition. They have high-explosive ammunition; they also have, you know, air-bursts, and so on, they can fire; all the way up to nuclear weapons, obviously, howitzers can to that. But say on a house, a weapon such as a howitzer would undoubtedly penetrate the house and explode, perhaps not knock the entire house down, but would do a lot of damage to the inside and to the outside structure of the house as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What about if you fire a tank round into a house?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, tank rounds also have ammunition which has high-explosive capability, and the effect there would be the same as what I've described. They also have anti-tank ammunition, which is more of a very hard projectile that is -- makes holes in tanks, essentially, through armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if anybody were, for some reason, to shoot something like that at a house, what would it do?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, again, an anti-tank weapon would make a hole in the outside structure, probably not cause too much damage inside, although, you know, certainly the person would feel it that it came through the walls, whereas a high-explosive burst would probably go through a wall and explode.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In paragraph 37 of your statement, there's a reference to a vehicle called a BMP. What is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: A BMP is a tracked air -- armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what is the difference between that and a BRMP that you refer to in paragraph 44 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: BRDM, I think -- let me just see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: BRM -- is it P --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: BRDM is essentially an air and also an armoured personnel carrier, but it's wheeled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, while we are on the topic of military equipment, although maybe slightly different, but to your knowledge, do night-vision binoculars have a range?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Much like a day binocular, they would have a range of several kilometres, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that generally when provoked, or perceived to be provoked -- sorry, I'm moving off the equipment, as such. You say in your statement that the movement of the VJ generally, when perceived to be provoked or being provoked, would respond in a disproportionate manner. Could you explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I guess in several incidents that I saw, there would be no -- they would not stand for provocation and provocation could be a very simple activity or could be, obviously, an act by the KLA, by the Albanian forces that would -- you know, might go as far as killing soldiers. And then the response seemed to me to be at all times much greater than the actual act that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can you mention any specific examples of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, you know, I can certainly -- I think it was on the 8th of January when a convoy of MUP police was ambushed by the KLA and two -- two MUP policemen were killed. The response was that some tanks came out of the Dulje position, VJ tanks, and started firing into a village that conceivably had no part in that ambush. And it just seemed to be an irrational but overwhelmingly greater response to that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think I'll couple that, in light of the objections we have. You state in your statement that the VJ and the MUP appeared to have a high level of coordination and collaboration in some operations. What is the basis for that assessment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the incident I just described here, obviously the MUP were the ones that were attacked, that were ambushed by the KLA and lost individuals; and the reaction was from the VJ. So somehow information was passed and coordination took place to react to the incident, certainly by my reading. And, of course, in other cases I can say, for example, the Rogovo incident, where the VJ was tracking, I believe, and actually at the border our assessment was what they -- is that they had seen the border intrusion by the KLA and the movement of the KLA across the border, and the VJ had tracked these folks along the way; but then the actual action in the Rogovo village was done by the MUP. So this is -- this certainly pointed to me that there was a level of coordination between the two forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And on this -- the Rogova incident, you say that the VJ was tracking some KLA members and then the MUP took over. Were you informed that -- by anyone that it was the same unit, that it was the same KLA group that had crossed the border and then eventually was taken --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, in fact in my meeting with Colonel Delic, I believe it's on the 1st of February, he refers to that, and his view was that it was the same -- it was the same group. In fact, he had -- his forces had actually killed three of the intruders in Pastrik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for your reference, this meeting is recorded in Exhibit MM/6 -- sorry, MM/6A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're tendering that sort of exhibit as appended to this statement rather than giving it a separate exhibit number, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My intention was that we would put in the whole bundle because every document, except for one, has been specifically referred to in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'll refer to the Milosevic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Listen to my question. You're not asking for separate exhibit numbers. These are just part of the statement, annexes to the statement, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all I need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: One exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need to know how you're doing it. I don't need to know any more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, as you told us, you were earlier in a -- you come out of a tank unit, if I understand you correctly. Based on your experience, would use of ammunition by a unit be reported up through the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mean, any time -- certainly in any militaries that I've served with, and that includes the French and the Canadian and the American military, alongside those other militaries, as soon as a round is expended, they are very tightly controlled, and so as soon as ammunition is used, there's a report done. And certainly when you're in an action as well, there is a contact report and a whole procedure that takes place when, actually, real weapons are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And why do you have that kind of mechanism in place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, it's to ensure that there's control of the ammunition and control of its use, particularly, and whether it's on a range or whether it's an actual operation. There's a very tight control so the ammunition doesn't get lost, first of all, and go into the wrong hands, and also that it's used appropriately, in accordance with the rules of engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't know if you can answer this, but would it sort of be possible to have tank ammunition and the like used at sort of private initiative, without people further up the chain knowing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Not in a disciplined military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, sort of flowing from this notion of rogue elements or private initiative, how would an officer, in your experience, react if he became aware that he had rogue elements among his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you answer that -- before you answer that question, which is moving on to a different subject, is your comment about the recording of the use of ammunition confined to heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It would be confined to any use of live ammunition. Live ammunition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At all --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- In most militaries is very carefully controlled for the reasons I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So if an officer becomes aware that among his subordinates he have rogue elements, either units or individuals, what would an officer do?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, certainly any officer, I believe, any professional officer, would deal very seriously and quickly and with a great deal of seriousness with -- you know, about this. And it could go as far as removing the rogue elements themselves, a rogue unit, but usually it's individuals, and all the way to disciplinary procedures that would be -- that would take place. But the first thing that undoubtedly would happen would be the removal of the person or unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you say "removal," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I mean pulling it back, taking it out of contact, taking it out of its mission, and moving it back, replacing it by other individuals or units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is that something that's -- is that just sort of commonly known practice or are these kinds of things taught at military academies as to how you should react?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, obviously, we used to think that it was a commonly known practice, but we found out very quickly that you need to even go further; and that is, not only do you teach it at basic training, both for enlisted soldiers and officers, but we also now -- we actually write it out in terms of the proper rules of engagement. We give every soldier, sailor, and airman a card that lays out his -- the rules of engagement card, that says, you know, that this is how you're going to behave in terms of behaviour with the threat, with the enemy, with the opposing forces as required. So this is a very tightly controlled, again, aspect of military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, you also described something -- you refer in paragraph 18 of your statement to frequent intimidations. What kind of actions are you referring to there, frequent intimidations on the part of the MUP and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, we had numerous reports of Albanians being beaten, being -- shoved around. For example, at check-points, examples of ID cards and other identification, driver's licences being taken away for no -- for no obvious reason and not returned. And, you know, people then were asked to show up and were asked for receipts that were never given. This kind of intimidation. In fact, I was personally -- I personally saw -- I went to a MUP station once where Albanian folks were lined up to receive -- to -- for administration purposes, for papers, et cetera. And the MUP policemen who were, you know, outside the station, you know, the -- none of the Albanians were looking up at them. They were -- you know, they were in a -- kind of almost a sheepish kind of a role there, and so certainly seemed to me to be intimidated by the authority -- the authority forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And Have you any experience with any VJ or MUP, how the VJ and MUP were respecting local customs as to how you would behave in social settings or traditions?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, I specifically remember going to visit an Albanian family with a Serb policeman -- or a Serb officer. And as you know, the custom in Albanian families was when you walk into the house you would remove your footwear. And of course as a -- you know, as an officer and a brigadier general at the time, even I took my footwear off. I used to always do it. It was just a common politeness and practice to walk into the house, and this Serb officer did not remove his footwear. He just walked in with his big boots and -- you know, to the consternation of the Albanian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Colonel Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It was a visit -- I don't remember exactly the location, but I was -- I remember visiting with him at this particular house and what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember whether it was up in the border area or was it --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe it was in the border area and we were looking at mechanisms for controlling the border and whether -- we had been pressing to have freedom of movement in the border area and we were discussing this with Colonel Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like now to show you a bit of -- well, it's the same exhibit so it's P2772.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what I'd like to show to the witness is page 73 of this exhibit. It is marked as MM/6 is the attachment to the statement. Can we spin this around so it's ... Could we zoom in on the lower half of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I don't know if you can read what's there right now. I see on my, screen there's a sentence beginning: "My family -- my family is now in Belgrade" --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: "My family is now in Belgrade. I have emotional connection to these territories. We all (Serbs) will protect Kosovo with our lives, historical monuments, and heritage."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this is Delic saying this at a meeting on the 26th of December --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- 1998? Would other Serb officers or people you interacted with express the same kind of views?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I believe this reflects the views of most of the, if not all of the Serbs that I dealt with in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your -- in different parts of your evidence, both in your statement and in your -- in the transcript of the Milosevic case, you discuss the border area and this 5-kilometre-wide border areas. Were restrictions placed on the movement of KVM in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, very heavy restrictions. We were not allowed to -- the arrangement was that we were not allowed to have freedom of movement -- the arrangement -- I should say the arrangement that we were told by the Serbs was that we would require a liaison officer, that we would plan ahead and have this liaison officer accompany us to the border areas. So we had totally restricted access.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I believe you described that in paragraph 24 of your statement. Now, how did those restrictions affect the ability of the KVM to carry out its mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, it affected it a great deal, and of course when we would receive reports from the Serb side that there were infiltrations across the border, there was no way for us to verify that or, for that matter, to verify the actions of the Serbs to counter those incursions. So that was -- you know, it was a very difficult way for us -- we were not in a position to do our job with respect to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your region -- you're responsible for the Prizren region?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you able to give an approximate sort of ratio between the area where you had unrestricted movement and how much was actually taken up by the border?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Maybe 10, 15 per cent of my area -- but I had one of the two areas -- two regions that had a border with Albania there. So it was a -- you know, a very serious and delicate -- sensitive area of Kosovo because of the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your statement you -- there's a quote from Exhibit MM/6A.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And it -- that says that "Loncar is not my commander," Loncar being the overall coordination liaison officer in Prizren, I believe. What -- can you -- what does that mean, "he's not my commander," if you understand that statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yeah, this was a discussion with Delic. I was trying to get -- I was trying to open up a field office in Planeja, which was in the 5-kilometre border area, and I was pressing him and trying to get this field office opened and he was saying at this point that he did not have the authority to decide that on his own. And I was telling him that General Loncar in Pristina had agreed to this and was, you know -- it had been negotiated with KVM headquarters itself and that he -- you know, he agreed with this. Now, at this point Colonel Delic told me that Loncar is not his commander, he's just a liaison officer, which kind of surprised me, because of course, I would have expected that General Loncar would have had the necessary authority to speak on behalf of the commander. If he's not the commander himself, that he would have had the necessary authority to speak on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did that affect your ability to carry out the mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, yeah. We continued to press to try this -- to have this office opened in Planeja. And the approach that I took and I think that the KVM generally approached, but I must say my regional centre had a chance to actually put this into effect more than the others, was to have decentralised locations where we could protect the populations and look after them and that is not just the Albanian populations but also the Serb populations in certain areas where they must be isolated within a pool of Albanians. So I was trying to really protect the people. In fact, I was quite worried that if there was eventually an agreement, there would be a heavy back-lash against the Serb population, so I was trying to open field offices in mainly Serb areas, went on Serb television, et cetera, and so trying to be impartial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to page 85 of the exhibit we have up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like, General, if you can help us decipher a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And can we spin this a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On your screen can you see this map?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I have it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this is a map that you provided to -- with your statement, it's MM/9. And it shows out-of-barrack locations of the VJ, places where the VJ has deployed outside of barracks. What I would like to seek your help on is to understand the different flags or boxes that we see on the map. Some of the boxes have three dots above them. What does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That indicates a platoon organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if there's a vertical line?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: One line is a company and two lines is a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And Some of these ones have a small bracket with a minus --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: With a minus, and it's just slightly less than a battalion but not quite, so it's not quite a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then inside these -- what is the right term for this, are they flags or are they boxes?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: They're, you know, symbols, I guess we'd call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Call them symbols.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yeah, symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, inside the square symbols we have sort of an oval shape?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. That indicates a battalion unit -- sorry, a tank unit. The ones that have just a cross indicates infantry. The ones that have a cross and a circle, an oval, indicates mechanised infantry. And the one that has a bridge or an E sideways is an engineering unit. And when there's no symbol above the little box, it's because there's an unknown size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look at Djakovica --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You have two small dots --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- below. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's motorised infantry. That would be on trucks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I would like if we could now move to the next page of this exhibit. If you could move it upright again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this is MM/10 attached to your statement, and it's the notes of a meeting on the 5th of February with the head of the MUP in Prizren who was also the deputy prefect. Now, could you place this document in context. What else was going on? Was there any significant events going on around this time, the 5th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The 5th of February, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, of course, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: There was -- of course we had had the Rogovo incident just before that, and there was a check-point in Rastane that was -- by our reading was oppressive or was checking more vehicles than it should have, and so I was trying to meet with the chief of police to try to get him to relax that -- to slow down and to reduce, I guess, the number of -- the number of checks, vehicle checks that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And on the international level, am I right, this is also around the time of the beginning of the Rambouillet negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, down in paragraph 6 at the bottom of the page there is mention of a MUP patrol going between Orahovac and Studencane. Am I correct that the MUP -- sorry -- the KVM had been following this patrol regularly. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, this was an agreed patrol. It was within the agreement, and so it was a regular patrol and it was -- we would not really escort but we would follow the patrol to ensure that nothing happened or if something happened we would be -- we would be in a position to see it. Of course this was meant to be a regular patrol that would use regular -- a regular route, and the route had changed, and this was causing some frustration and -- to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why had the route changed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like us now to look at page 98 of the same exhibit, and this is MM/13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, when -- during proofing did you have a chance to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And this is a document. There are three different versions of the document.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct. Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, when we -- of course, when we developed records of discussion, I had taken some notes, the note-taker had, and if any other persons were in the room, they had also taken notes, so would try to put everything together to have an accurate read-out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. By your leave, in our submission, written submission we objected to MM/13 and all the documents attached thereto. As far as I can see my learned friend Mr. Marcussen is examining based on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think that's consistent with the decision we've made that we'll allow the examination and then we'll deal with the issues of objections once everyone's had a chance to review the position clearly. Sometime this afternoon this will all be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, just so we now what is the correct version, am I correct then that then the last of the three versions --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The signed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- the one that's signed --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The signed version is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could go to -- to page 106 of this exhibit, please. This is MM/13A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is a reference here -- this is -- you described this in your evidence, but this is a report you made I believe on the 16th about the events on the 15th and 16th --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- at Racak. The thing I wanted to clarify with you is about -- well, the first line on -- no, sorry. About two-thirds down on the page there is a sentence -- a bullet point beginning: "One team from CC3 is near 122-millimetre position (3)." What is a 122-millimetre position?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That was a howitzer position, presumably of three howitzers which were -- appeared getting ready to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And this is on the 16th, on the day when the investigation judge -- there's a debate about the -- the modalities of the investigation judge going in and investigating Racak.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I think this is the day before --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes. My question actually was this: Is -- were those weapons, to your knowledge, actually fired on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I can't say whether they were or not. I cannot say for sure whether they were or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm still trying to find this reference. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the first page, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The first page of the document which have -- is attachment number MM/13A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 13A, sorry. Just a second. Did you say there are three versions of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Oh, no, sorry. There are three versions of attachment MM/13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: A two-page version, a three-page version, and then another three-page version that's signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the one I should be looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is two --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If ultimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If ultimately we are going to work off attachment P2772, then the third version is beginning at e-court page 103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just want to know what page of the documents I've got in front of me this is on. Everything's so complicated. Who actually signed the document did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: CP Weisflogg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Weisflogg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Weisflogg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the passage begins with what words?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, sir. That's something -- we then moved on to the next attachment which is 13A which is where I made reference to the 122-millimetre weapon. Now, if it's of assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is 13A in relation to 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 13A is the witness's report about the incidents in Racak on 15th and 16 January. It's a different document. I might have been moving too fast. I was just trying to sort out which document we should be referring to when we look at attachment 13. And just wanted to clarify why it is there are three versions of that. And then I moved on to another attachment, and what I was trying to get clarification on there is the kind of weapon that's referred to. I'm sorry if I've confused matters by moving through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, when did you leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I left Kosovo -- I believe it was about the 15th of March on my leave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- were you part of -- were you back so that you were part of the evacuation of the KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I was not. The mission was evacuated before I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you return to the mission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I did return to the mission and met with my verifiers in Ohrid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where is that, what country?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: In FYROM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where did you -- what function did you have in the KVM after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, after a period of discussion, the Permanent Council of the OSCE decided to organise a mission to go into Albania to deal with the refugee -- the refugee crisis that was going on. And so they asked me to organise a force, the OSCE-KVM Refugee Task Force in Albania, which I did, and we deployed to Albania shortly after the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what kind of functions did you carry out there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The mission had three distinct functions. First, it was a fairly wide mandate to assist the Government of Albania with the refugee crisis; the second was to take statements on the atmosphere and the treatment of the refugees before their departure from Kosovo and the reasons why they were leaving Kosovo and coming across; and the third was to prepare for a possible registration of the refugees in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you carry out all three functions?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Certainly in the time that I was there -- I left in the middle of May. By the time I left, we had certainly, I believe, assisted a great deal the Albanian government in dealing with the refugee crisis. We deployed teams throughout the entire country in every prefecture to provide support, assistance, counselling, and communications coordination. But also, the second mission of taking statements, we took a great number of statements, in the hundreds, from different refugees that had come across. And the third mission, certainly by the time I left we had not yet got to -- the registration piece had not yet been filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe how these statements were taken. Now, first of all, how were the people who were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I see my colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By all means, finish the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- please sit down just now, Mr. Ivetic. I have a question I want to ask. What was your personal involvement with the refugees in the exercise of taking statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I, as the head of the Refugee Task Force, I travelled every day and met with refugees in different places, either in refugee camps, in make-shift gathering locations, such as the local sports complex in Tirana, and on the road I went to the border on several occasions with -- the border with Kosovo. And so I was -- I met with refugees every single day. As well, many of them came to my office, because of course they would recognise the orange vehicles that we were using as the ones that had been in Kosovo and there was certainly a connection there. And many of them certainly -- many of our local employees that we had employed in Kosovo, you know, tried to find us and would come to our office and make contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over what period of time did you have daily meetings with refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the moment we got there, I personally got there, I believe about the 3rd of April until the moment I left on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe that the area that counsel has embarked upon is an area that we've already covered. We've made reference to it in our motion but it's something that Your Honour has already ruled on previously, the inadmissibility of certain evidence relating to interviews conducted by the OSCE outside of the boundaries of Yugoslavia, and I believe that we need to address this matter, then, because this type of material has previously been excluded and for the same reasons that we set forth previously, continual reference to such material and talking in general terms that cannot be verified where statements were not under oath, the declarants are not identified, et cetera, causes, we believe -- infringes greatly upon the rights of the accused in this case to be able to confront the evidence against them and in that sense would infringe upon the proceedings of things. So I have to bring this up at this time, because up until now I think the questions have been permissible but now this line of questioning goes into the areas that have already been -- ad nauseam I believe been dealt with in prior hearings on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, two points. The so-called Blue Book of the KVM was admitted into evidence, and we had a specific debate about the parts of the Blue Book that summarises what some of these refugees told the KVM had happened to them in Kosovo. Those parts were allowed in. You might recall we had in that context a discussion about how these statements -- facts were ranked pursuant to a standard intelligence ranking system where information was sort of given A1, A2, A3 depending on its reliability and credibility. Those parts were allowed in. So evidence of this nature is admissible and has been admitted already in this case. Now, secondly, what I was going to come to and Your Honour already picked up on it, this witness spoke to numerous persons who had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before we go into that. Mr. Maisonneuve, there is a matter here I think which should be debated without you being in the courtroom, so the usher will escort you out briefly while we deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness himself spoke to numerous witnesses, witnesses that he himself went up and, so to speak, picked and had conversations with through an interpreter. So this witness is able to give -- it's hearsay but it's first-hand hearsay evidence summarising what he was told about the conditions under which the refugees he spoke to left Kosovo. And what I intended to do, just to let Your Honours in on what's going to happen next is, I intended to show two KVM reports, MM/15 and MM/16 to the witness which basically are a summary of what refugees had told the KVM in these questionnaires. And I think the witness's personal experience confirming what is in these documents supports the reliability of these documents that I'm going to put to the witness. Basically they say that the KVM spoke to several hundred refugees from Kosovo. They -- they had been exposed to extreme violence and brutality, they were forced out of their homes and told to leave Kosovo. Now, the issue all this goes to is, of course -- the issue all this goes to is the issue of whether -- of the reasons why these hundreds of thousands of refugees left Kosovo. So it goes to an important issue in the Prosecution's case, obviously. And we submit that if there are issues about the hearsay nature of this evidence, those would be things that goes to weight rather than admissibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Something additional, Mr. Sepenuk, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you don't mind. The MM/15, I don't know if the Tribunal's had a chance to look at it yet -- whether Chamber's had a chance to look at it, but it is a mini-As Seen, As Told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it in front of me. I know the nature of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. There's one thing, just for ease of reading, and I think I'm right on this. The first page is K0075721, if that's true on Your Honour's, and then the next page is actually K0075726. The next page is the last page, for ease of reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not in my copy. I have 22 as the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, but it says: "During the first few days of the NATO bombing which began on March 24th," down at the bottom of 5721, if Your Honour sees that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it says: "The." And then you turn to the next page and suddenly there are these bullet points. Is that correct on yours, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. That's just not correct. You should go to K0075726, that's actually the next page. It's just the OTP simply got it out of order. It just makes for much easier reading. That's all I want to point out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The difference between this and what has happened before is that the witness appears to have personal knowledge of interviewing refugees, and counsel will remember that some of the material that Abrahams could speak to directly was admitted. In addition, in the decision that we made in relation to As Seen, As Told and Under Orders, we made it clear that the documents themselves or the evidence contained in the documents themselves was admissible in respect that it was compiled by an outside body. We chose not to admit it because of our dissatisfaction with what had been established about its reliability. Whether the position is any different in relation to the exhibits here which Mr. Marcussen wishes to associate with the witness's own personal evidence remains to be determined once we've heard what we can say, not only about his own personal experience in interviewing refugees, but also about the compilation of these two documents. So again we will reserve our decision in relation to these until we've heard examination and cross-examination. This is rather different from the Racak point. We might be able to decide it after lunchtime. But this one will depend on hearing the whole of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. One other point that I wanted to just point out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ivetic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I only wanted to add that the page -- the second page of the exhibit and which I can focus on where the bullet points start at the bottom of the page, the -- one of the main problems we have is that we cannot even tie necessarily all of the observations or discussions that General Maisonneuve had with refugees to incidents from the indictment. Here we have reference to various allegations of crimes in places such as Vranisht, Gjeshko, Trnje, Lesha, et cetera, which are not in the indictment or at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some of these we've heard evidence about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Some we have, right, and some we have not, so that's my concluding point to point out to Your Honours, as I'm sure you'll consider all the objections at the proper time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: May I just point out that the allegation in the indictment that 800.000 people were expelled from Kosovo is not limited to 800.000 people from the locations of the specific crime sites. So the Kosovo transfer and deportation count is broader than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, that may be so. The issue here is a rather different one from simply relying on that broad general averment, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will continue with the evidence, Mr. Maisonneuve. Thank you for your patience. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I think I was about to ask you about how the interviews that were made by -- no, sorry, that was not -- I was about to ask you how the refugees that were interviewed by the KVM were selected.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, what we tried to do was when we'd speak to the refugees we would try to pick out of a crowd or find out from the crowd any of the refugees that had specific information and had, if you wish, specific evidence of what they had witnessed personal -- personally witnessed. And then we would take them apart from the rest of the group and speak to them with an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how would those interviews be recorded?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: We had a form that we filled out, that the verifiers filled out, after discussing, you know -- this form, this was a regular form with all the necessary information with a specific statement. And then the verifier would sign at the bottom and usually the witness as well, the refugee as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you yourself take any statements?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Actually, I did. I took one statement just to get a feel for what my verifiers were going through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you mentioned this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify something. When we dealt with As Seen, As Told, one of our findings was that the information was anonymous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think -- anonymous not in the sense that the name of the source was not recorded in the questionnaires. In As Seen, As Told there is no reference to the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And all these documents have now been disclosed, have they?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I believe so. Unless something else -- what has been disclosed is these print-outs from this database we have have been disclosed in redacted form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do they identify the personnel -- the refugees who were giving the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, because they are redacted. What has been disclosed is redacted for the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the significance of the signing of a statement with a name on it? Was this just to do with the reliability of the information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This witness only did one statement himself and we have plenty more evidence about how that was generated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Not in evidence. We do have it. It's just for the Court to know that this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you do these basic things like give him the statement that he actually compiled and let him at least verify it. It's progress long the road. It's this lack of concentration on the sorts of things that you expect to be proved in a court that is so frustrating in this case. Anyway, carry on with what you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General -- so you mentioned that you spoke to other refugees. So am I correct that that was not in the context of taking actual statements as such?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You spoke to --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would speak to them, find out how they were, how they were treated. And I had, as I say, daily contact with refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were there any selection process there or how did your contact with these people --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No. I would just walk around and speak to them and meet with them and I just generally asked how they were and how they had been treated and what they had and what their condition was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- from those discussions you had with these refugees, were there certain -- were there patterns emerging from those as to the condition under which the refugees had left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, there were. First of all, they had left not for their own reasons. They had been forcibly forced to leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may find this a very difficult exercise and I'm sorry if it may seem unrealistic to you, but there are sound reasons why I'm asking you to do this. Can you distinguish conclusions you arrived at from your own personal inquiries from those that you might have reached by reading summaries of the accumulated statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you understand -- I hope you do understand the point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that is concerning us, and that is the anonymity of so much of the material that might be presented which is different -- although you don't know the names of the refugees you spoke to, the way in which you did it might give the evidence a different weight from evidence that we think really can't be challenged at all. So could you try in your answer to distinguish what you learned personally --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- from what you discovered from looking at other people's recorded statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give you two specific examples. In Tirana there's a sports complex, an interior sports complex in which I went and actually spoke to a number of refugees there. For example, at this one -- in this particular sports complex I met a young man probably 15-years-old, an Albanian who had lost contact with his family and told stories of him being pushed out and having to walk from his home across the border and, you know, joining a group of refugees. Then specifically in my office in Tirana I had two young men come and call on me, young men who had actually been -- who were Albanian and who had been my security -- part of my security personnel local employees in Kosovo, in Prizren, and they walked in and told me of their -- what had happened with them. They had gone across -- had been pushed across, forced across the border. One of them had a young -- a young wife and a young baby, and both of them were in -- currently in a refugee accommodation in Tirana. And in fact, those two young men were coming to tell me that they were going to join the KLA. I mean, both of those specific incidents that I personally of course am privy to had a real emotional effect on me and that's why I remember them very specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are, though, willing to hear evidence, Mr. Marcussen, of a more general nature based on personal experience, if you do want to pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my intention, to try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do you accept that in relation to the forms, you've advanced the matter no further than it was the state of play when we made our earlier decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My intention was not to try to change that decision; it was just to put in context what the general had been involved in. It was not to try to change anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, now from -- if -- as Judge Bonomy said, if it's possible for you to try to disregard the different aggregated information you saw in reports, but just thinking about the people you actually spoke to yourself. From those interactions and discussions with people, could you give a general description of what they told you about the conditions under which they left.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right. The general context was that all the ones that I spoke to told me that they had been forced to pick up whatever they could carry on their person or in their vehicle and would have come across -- had been pushed cross the border, forced to come across the border with Albania. This was a generalised -- every time I spoke to them -- and this is not from any aggregated report, this is the story I got -- that generally that they would come across, that their papers had been taken from them, sometimes their licence plate removed from their vehicle and had been told to carry on down the road towards Albania. And of course, Prizren had a direct line or a direct road into Albania, so I knew exactly, you know, the road that they had been forced to take, but that was the general information I received from all the refugees that I spoke to, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- were you told who had told the refugees to leave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It wasn't specific in terms of, you know, people, but it was most -- I would qualify it as Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were you told about other things than just being -- people being told that they had to leave and go to Kosovo [sic]. Were you told about --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Well, this is the place I guess where I -- I have a hard time distinguishing between what I heard in -- what I read in my reports and what I was told personally, and I would not venture there but of course, I have -- we were told many times of some of the treatment that they suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we could see now exhibit -- sorry, the same exhibit, so P2772, page 115, please, and this is this attachment MM/15. And I thank my learned colleague, Mr. Sepenuk, for finding out that there's indeed been an unfortunate shuffling of the pages when this was initially scanned into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This document, you provided it to the Office of the Prosecutor, so I take it that I am going to be correct to say that you are familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how this document was compiled.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: This document was compiled by my staff in the Refugee Task Force based on the statements that we had been taking and our assessment of the situation in Kosovo at the time the refugees were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is this a document that at the time you approved? I see it's a Human Rights Biweekly Report. Is that said something --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So in your view, does this express -- reflects -- sorry. Is this a correct reflection of what the KVM was being told by refugees in Albania --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It's an exact reflection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this is from sort of the beginning of the period, from the 2nd through the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we can look now, staying on the same exhibit, page 121, please. And this is attachment M/16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: This was -- as I mentioned before, I departed the mission on the 12th of May, so I wanted to -- before I left, I wanted to provide a progress report on the mission, the overall mission that the Refugee Task Force had been undertaking and this was the progress report that I provided to the OSCE headquarters in Vienna. So this was unfiltered, this was a report that was compiled by my staff and which I approved before it was sent up to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so this report, is that correct to say, that it covers the period from early April and up through the first --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct. And the way we tried to divide it up is to have a kind of general section at the beginning and then try to cover every province of Albania specifically in the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so the information included in this document has the information we had in the first document plus additional information you had gathered for another month?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can look at page 129, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page of the document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is page 8 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There you describe in the second section B, the human rights situation in Kosovo. Now, again, does this reflect your view of the situation in Kosovo based on what you had been informed by the refugees that you and KVM was in contact with?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll have to object to the question. He's using "you." I think he has to specify between what the general himself heard and what his team may have heard, because I think it makes a difference in the long run as to how this is viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is meant to be the foundation for the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What we have is we have the head of the task force receiving information from his staff that had been asking witnesses questions plus himself speaking to refugees all over Albania in refugee camps and wherever they were. So the question is whether this exhibit reflects his understanding of how the events had been in Kosovo when the refugees left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's already answered that question because he's told you that's his report on leaving, his report to Vienna, compiled by his staff but expressing the position as it was then. So you have the answer, and beyond that I don't think it's appropriate to go. It's a suitable time to interrupt, if it's convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Actually, this finishes my examination of the witness, so it is indeed. I have -- I had prepared -- sorry, this is an administrative matter just -- it can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have to break at this stage for an hour for lunchtime. Again, please, Mr. Maisonneuve, the usher will show you where to go in the interim. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had prepared before coming today an overview of where in the Maisonneuve statements and in the Milosevic transcript the different exhibits that I attached to the statement are referred as I guess a lot of people would be working on these sort of issues maybe over the break in the context I was prepared to hand out copies to the Defence and Your Honours if it would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The usher has left. I'll make sure that it gets to you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, can you assist us now more specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I shall do my best, Your Honour. I'll address the transcript references in the order that they appear in the motion, paragraph 3 of the motion. I believe Your Honours have already dealt with the first objection, that will be to page 5780 -- sorry, 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, there's a big chunk of the transcript being objected to in the second row of the table, pages 5778 to 5805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in my submission, all of those pages should go in, they're all relevant, and I'll set out the specific topics that I think I addressed in various parts of this section of the transcript. For example, at paragraph -- at page 5779 we have the issue of tanks at Racak firing into houses where there were people and the fact that the verifiers saw that. That run over a couple of pages. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's specifically looking the events of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right. What we -- it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is no evidence presently before the Trial Chamber of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What we are relying on is the fact that there was a VJ tank involved in the operation and that it fired during the operation. And I don't know how we can lead that evidence without getting into what happened in Racak. There were tanks; they were involved in the operation. That's what this evidence shows or that we rely on it for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not going to look at the Racak operation, so end of story on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, in our submission it's relevant to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe it is, but it's out of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But there's another issue in the case, which is who were in control of the operations that carried out in Kosovo from March 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're going to invite us to consider hearsay evidence of this nature about the presence of these tanks firing into houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, not only hearsay evidence, evidence from various officers found in attachments 13, 13A, 13B, and these other exhibits, MM/8 and MM/7 that there were tanks involved in the operation in Racak. Now, I'm fully aware that we're -- and we're not trying to engage in an exercise where we want the Trial Chamber to make findings whether there were 40 or 50 people killed and whether they were KLA or not and all that. We're aware of the fact that the count is out of the indictment, but there are other issues arising from what happened in Racak. This is the first big event in 1999, and it shows the continued pattern of VJ and MUP cooperation. And this instance -- it shows cooperation, it shows excessive use of force, this witness is saying firing a tank into a civilian house is not proportionate force in these kind of circumstances. The verifiers that were at Racak saw this tank fire and subsequently went down to the house and helped -- the people who were in the house had been hiding in the basement and he -- they went down and helped them out of the basement. Now, what does that evidence go to? It only goes to the fact that there was a VJ involvement in Racak. But that would, according to this witness, have been something that would have had to have been coordinated at at least the brigade level, maybe higher, on military side and at MUP headquarters in Pristina. That's why we are putting forward this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, continue if you wish, but I certainly am not persuaded by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I'll make my submissions and then we'll see where it takes us. Paragraph 5782, the witness explained that firing a tank at a house is excessive use of force. Paragraph 5786 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you move further, from line 24 on 5781 to line 8 on -- line 9 on 5783 seems to me to be perfectly general evidence that this witness can give.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, but if -- my submission on this chunk of evidence is that if there's anything that should go out here, we wouldn't object to taking out pages 5795, line 8, to the following page, line 10, which is this thing about where the bodies were lying, in the gully and these sorts of things. This -- we understand this is getting into the nitty-gritty of what happened and things like that and that should go out. All the other parts of this evidence -- although there's some descriptions of what happened at Racak, they all go to these coordination issues, who were involved, how many forces were involved, and I can go through, I mean, all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, I have to say I thought your problem was resolved by if you go to the page of -- the foot of 5783, line 19 -- or, in fact, line 20: "During the remainder of your stay in Kosovo were there other times when you saw Serb forces direct heavy weapons against civilian structures?" And he answers that. Now, why do you need any more than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, just checking the precise reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seemed to be the modus -- he said this in his evidence anyway. "It seemed to be the modus operandi of the Serb security forces that any type of provocation, no matter how small, would result in an overwhelming use of force disproportionate to the actions of the KLA or other perpetrators, and this was constantly one of the things that I reinforced to the Serbs but also to the KLA when I met them, saying 'I don't know why you're provoking them' because you know that it always results in disproportionate use of force."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He then gives an example which he's also given today in his evidence. This next part is already in evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right, I led that today obviously because I wasn't sure how -- what was going to get in. It's difficult when you present a witness under 92 ter and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then you see it goes wrong again because it says "returning to the 15th of January for a moment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, my submission about that again is -- it is the context in which this operation was carried out -- yeah, my part is simply the same. This evidence -- there are a few pages that we submit should be taken out; the rest of it is all relevant to the issues that I've mentioned. And what I intended to do was to give some headlines to different pages where different issues in our submission begin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- and explain the relevance of those ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, on you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So at -- just to be clear, I'm giving headings and then normally the issue will run over a couple of pages. So at page 5786 we have a discussion of the attachment MM/8 in which Petrovic confirms VJ involvement. At page 578 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. Where line on 5786?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's -- begins at line 15. One of the problems with the transcript is there's no reference to the specific attachments, which is why I handed outline this overview just before the break. But what is being discussed there at paragraph -- from paragraph -- sorry, line 15 or 16 is MM/8. Now, Petrovic confirms VJ involvement. On page 5789 we have reference to -- at line 8 to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is Petrovic? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Petrovic was the liaison officer for the -- for the combat team, the tank teams that were at Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At page 5789, line 8, Jelesic, and that is the commander of the combat team, is explaining that -- well, what is in the underlying document is that he is saying, well, we were conducting our training operations up on the rim, the MUP was doing something down in the gully -- down in Racak and this was unconnected. And the witness offered the explanation at page 5790, beginning at line 14, that this is such a far-fetched suggestion that things would have happened that way, that he simply finds that utterly unbelievable. It would be such a risk of, as he called it, blue-on-blue, people shot by their own people if you did something like that and that's utterly unbelievable. He then offers on the next page at page -- at line 9 the opinion that an operation involving around a hundred MUP officers and tanks would have been something that's coordinated at the brigade level. Subsequent page we have discussions about the basis for the witness's knowledge that VJ did actually fire at a house at Racak. At page 5793, line 4, we have a discussion of attachment MM/13 where it's being confirmed by one of the officers involved that there were a hundred MUP plus VJ involvement. At paragraph -- that goes for some pages. Then at paragraph -- sorry, at page 5796 the witness says that he was told -- was that he recalls that men and women were being separated by the forces that operated in Racak. Now, some of this is underlying material for attachment MM/13A, which is the witness's assessment -- the report he drafted on the events at Racak and on the 15th and 16th of January, 1999, in which he offers the view that the VJ had, indeed, offered a long-range support for the MUP operation. And he describes this further at page 5798. Then at page 5800 we have a description of what happened on the 17th of March when the investigating judge Marinkovic moved in with a MUP team into Racak to carry out this investigation. Now, the Court has already heard evidence about this from other witnesses, Drewienkiewicz and I believe also Richard Ciaglinski. This evidence is allowed and this evidence is corroborating what we've already heard from these witnesses but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
