utterances.text: Sorry, what's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, this witness says that there was an act of provocation when the MUP -- the manner in which the MUP went into Racak to carry out the investigation. The MUP did not -- and the investigating judge did not accept the offer that the KVM could try to facilitate the investigation process by going in with the KVM and maybe a small protection team. The witness is saying moving in with -- a few days after the event at Racak moving in again with a heavy MUP presence was bound to draw shooting from the KLA, and true enough, did. Now, this tie-in with this issue of whether or not the forces of FRY and Serbia were acting in a provocative active way, and we've heard evidence from Drewienkiewicz that in his view, both the VJ and the MUP went looking for trouble and found it. He was, for example, talking about Podujevo. At paragraph -- at page 5804 there's an objection to a discussion of MM -- attachment MM/14 which contains a reference to the witness's complaints to Drinic at the KLA site about the way they conduct -- conducted themselves at Racak. This just goes to -- in our view, to the unbiased nature of the way the KVM was acting, if -- that's all we put that forward for. We are not proposing anything else. So that deals with the first big batch of objections. I believe Your Honour's also dealt with a second smaller one, namely the objection to page 5821, lines 17 through 23. But just to repeat our submission on this, this -- the evidence that's been discussed -- the issue that's been discussed at this part of the transcript is about the coordination -- it's about the cooperation of the commander of this combat team that was up on the rim of Racak. It has nothing to do with the specific events at Racak. Then there is an objection to another larger chunk of evidence, which is pages 5821 through 5853. And, now, here we would agree to leaving out page 5840, line 16, through 5844, line 7, and also 5844, line 24, to 5850, line 17. The rest in our submission is all relevant evidence for the following reasons: At page 5834 we get details about the verifiers that were on the ground and their ability to observe this tank unit and the firing at the house. We get evidence at page 5840 about the tanks actually shooting at the house. At page 5844 there's discussion of whether or not the victims were KLA. Now, it's not something that we as the Prosecution necessarily want to get into because we understand this is getting very close to the actual crime base evidence. The reason why we at this stage do object to the objection of this evidence is that we don't yet know what the Defence case is going to be. If the Defence case is going to be that all those who were killed at Racak were all KLA fighters, well then, we would like to have our evidence in from this witness as to what he saw about the victims but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would the Defence have evidence that everyone who was killed at Racak was a KLA fighter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't know the Defence case yet. It was Milosevic's suggestion that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it was a big issue in the Milosevic trial. Why would the Defence want to lead that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, they want to -- I'm speculating. My guess would be that they would be saying: Look, this was an entirely legitimate operation. The KVM went out there screaming and yelling that this was all a massacre, it wasn't true, there was a political motive behind it, these kind of issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't these very points just answer your submission completely that you can't actually address the Racak issue by looking at one tank that may have fired at a house and have to look at everything before you can do justice to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, on the specific tank issue this witness is saying that when you receive light-arm fire, you do not deploy a tank and shoot into a house. That's not how you do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need to hear about Racak to know that. He's told us that. What we're -- you're talking about now is a specific example of that being done, and that immediately opens the door to assessing or listening to all the evidence about how strong the KLA were in the locality and what the risks were for the Serb forces who might be carrying out the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it not? So you might be happy with that. As far as you're concerned, this looks to me like a backdoor attempt to introduce Racak. And if you wanted to introduce it, you should have applied to introduce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We're not attempting to try to revive the charges of murder in relation to Racak. I'm explaining why it is that we think there is a basis at this stage to allow in the evidence about -- the evidence as to why the witness say that in his view, the victims were not members of the KLA. We're anticipating the Defence's case. I think we have an obligation to do that. We're trying to do that. But if Your Honours think at this point that is pointless, then of course we will have to accept that. And the same may very well be the case with the next bit from this section of the transcript that I'm going to mention, namely, 5850, line 18, where the issue is whether or not Walker had a good-faith basis for saying that there was a massacre at Racak. There's some issues about what time different information was available to Walker and when he made his statement. Again, this is mainly evidence we want to anticipate what the Defence might be bringing in their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what basis, though, could that be an issue here? You can't just say: I'm frightened what the Defence will do, let me introduce everything I want. On what basis could you anticipate this as part of the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, there have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you not be objecting to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The objection to a whole range of -- as I'm trying to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, would you not be objecting to them trying to explore that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If they can establish a basis that's relevant to their case, such as, for example, whether or not there was actually bias on the part of the KVM, I suspect that will probably be allowed. Now we think it's -- there's no basis, as a matter of fact, for those propositions but we've seen cross-examination of a number of KVM officers -- senior officers being challenged on what you were just supporting the KLA, you were biased, you were not reporting. If those issues don't come up, then this kind of evidence is of no use. If they do come up, I guess the only other option would be to present it in the rebuttal case. The third row in this table is an objection to transcript pages 5855 through 5892. I think we are here in the part of the cross-examination, and having reviewed the evidence, there I think we're mainly having in this part of the transcript fightings between Milosevic and the Bench and repetitions of issues that have already been covered. So we would be amenable to agree to leaving that passage of the exhibits -- sorry, of the transcript out. And finally there's an objection to page 5903 through 5909. There I just have to look. I would -- this is, again, the issue of at what point in time Walker had -- there are different things, but we would still ask that pages 5904, line 16, through 5907, line 7, be allowed in. It's the same issue about at what time Walker had what information. My submissions are the same as I made on that point. The other parts of the objection to this particular section of the transcript we don't have any problems with. So that concludes my submission on the transcript. I'm sorry if it has been somewhat nitty-gritty and detailed, but there were a lot of different issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you have to deal with all the issues that were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, as to the statement -- I don't know whether you would like me to address that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The objection to paragraphs 30 through 36, well, we're really covering the same points that I've just been making in relation to the transcripts. The key point being made here is the -- whether or not the VJ was involved in the operation at Racak and in what function. There's a paragraph, like paragraph 36 -- 34, sorry, which really rather concerns the assistance rendered by KVM staff to people that had been injured in Racak is not something we should -- we are relying on for the purpose of our case. Something like that could -- could go out. Yeah. The rest I think goes to the issues that I've set out before. Paragraph 45 to 50, it's again the same issue and it's covering some of these same attachments, attachments 13, 13A, and 13B to the statement, and again, the issue here is whether or not there was VJ and MUP cooperation at Racak and whether or not excessive force was used. And I don't think there's any point in me repeating myself on this. We submit this as relevant to the Prosecution's case and should be allowed in. I want to reassure the Court we are not trying to get Racak in through the backdoor. We are seeing a different purpose for this evidence which goes to linkage, the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, the involvement of the accused in what we say was a coordinated campaign in Kosovo from at least March 1998 all the way through to the end of the indictment period. So I just want to re-emphasise that point again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about the other -- the final two exhibits in paragraph 7 and 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I thought I had -- I don't think I have anything to add to what I already submitted. I think I went through each of these exhibits and explained why they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, they may be a problem for you and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- with that in mind, if you try to obtain more evidence on this point from the personal knowledge of the witness, you would be well-advised to ask him further questions. You were seeking to ask whether this -- one or both of these documents were consistent with his own impression, and you were not allowed to ask that question. What you could have done, if you wanted to pursue the matter, was ask him what his impression was on circumstances in general under various headings if you feel that that's something you want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are we talking about exhibits? Maybe I'm confused. Exhibits or the final to exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: MM/15 and MM/16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's me misunderstanding what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To describe MM/16 as a -- I think it was MM/16 as a mini As Seen, As Told, well certainly the latter part of it is accurate and I think also that description was given to MM/15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I made submissions when there was an objection to the line of questions that were being pursued by me in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all I'm saying to you is if you have nothing further to say on that, you may be well-advised to ask further questions to get the witness's personal knowledge and experience in case these are excluded. I mean, you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, but I -- yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can reflect on that while I hear if there's anything else to be said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think in fairness to the Defence what the witness indicated was that he could say from his own knowledge, he could say that people had been evicted by forces of the FRY and Serbia but he was not in a position to say whether he knew from documents he had read or from his personal discussions with people, whether the more specific acts such as killings and things like that had taken place. So I think I will possibly -- I will have to leave it at this. If it is not a sufficient basis to get the documents in, we can only get in the evidence about people being forced to leave Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, MM/16 is a report he supervised the compilation of reporting on the situation as at the 11th of May, when he left. But it's a matter for you, obviously, to decide what course you want to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we've said it all, so I think that's -- we'll rest on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. All we're in a position to do at this stage is give parties guidance along the lines that we have -- or I have already tried to do to Mr. Marcussen in relation to the documents that can be compared to As Seen, As Told. And our decision will be consistent with the decision in As Seen, As Told, and therefore when we finalise it, it will exclude the sort of material that is contained in these documents that is of the same nature. So far as Racak is concerned, evidence of -- that goes to show coordination between the forces and the use of excessive force, in the restricted sense, that the Prosecution have referred to, namely, the use of heavy weaponry against domestic -- apparently domestic property, that general evidence we will admit. But so far as evidence going to the crime base, the murders in Racak is concerned, we will not be admitting that. Now, this -- the final actual exercise will require us to go through the various passages and issue an order which makes it clear which passages are -- and exhibits are not being taken into account and which are. And that will be done later today, if possible. It will certainly be done in the context of this witness's evidence so that no one's in any doubt before he finishes what the final position is. But it can't be done at this minute. So the witness will return now for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll be glad you've only had wars to fight. It looks like Mr. Sepenuk is kicking off for the Defence. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. I'm Norman Sepenuk and I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic, and I'm going to depart from what I thought was going to be sort of the traditional kind of cross-examination because something you said this morning really made me think about a few things. And you said that you were a -- you called yourself -- I think with a smile, you said: "I'm just a simple soldier." And I want to just talk about that for a minute and about the mind of a soldier, whether it be a Canadian soldier, an American soldier, or a Serbian soldier because I think you could give us perhaps unique insight into this subject we've heard little about. You've testified about a meeting you had with General Delic --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Colonel Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel Delic, excuse me. I have a habit of saying general which we don't have to go into it. The Court has already it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that because he's now General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, he is now General Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's what caused the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, of course, you've made rapid strides from a brigadier general to what you say lieutenant-general in just a few years. But in any event, I take it you regarded Colonel Delic as a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, just generally speaking, that the VJ, the army, cooperated with you and behaved, generally speaking, in a satisfactory manner during your three months in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say generally yes, although there was a difference between the way Delic did and the commander of the Urosevac Brigade did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You talk about Colonel Jelic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And without getting into --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And without getting into a debate about it because Colonel Jelic said he was out in the field and he couldn't see you -- he eventually did see you with Colonel Kotur a few weeks later. So there was a mix-up on that. But other than that, you were generally satisfied with their behaviour, they reacted in a professional manner and tried to do the right thing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the meeting you had with Colonel Delic, it's MM/6 at page 73, Mr. Marcussen was asking you about it. And the two of you, you and Colonel Delic, and I think Mr. -- Major -- was it Colonel, Major Morwood. Who else was there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Lieuteneant Colonel Morwood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He was also there. I think the two of you were trying to get to know one another. This was 10, 11 days after you got to the field. You started in Vienna then you went to Pristina, and then Prizren, December 15th in Prizren, and then you were there for about three months, you left March 15th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you're trying to get to know one another and you start to talk about terrorism and Colonel Delic said that, you know, we just can't tolerate terrorism. And you said, Well, we, too, in Canada don't tolerate armed resistance. Okay. And he says, Well, and we can't accept terrorism but he says, We won't provoke -- we will not provoke any kind of an incident. And then we get to the part that Mr. Marcussen asked you about, and again effort to get to know one another. And you said to the colonel, you said, Where are you from? And he said, Well, my family is now in Belgrade. I have emotional connection to these territories. We all. And it's underlined in the transcript here, we all, and then it says "(Serbs) will protect Kosovo with our lives historical monuments, and heritage." And then Mr. Marcussen went on to another subject. It sort of stopped there. Can you -- what was the significance of that to you, General? I mean, obviously there's a reason why Mr. Marcussen asked you the question, you gave the answer. And so can you just tell us what the significance of that was to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I think that showed me the level of emotional engagement and attachment that certainly Colonel Delic and -- by his implication that all Serbs have to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And isn't that sort of a natural thing. I mean, let me give you as an example. It sounds unimportant and it probably is in the general scheme of things. I was struck by your Initial Impressions. You wrote this document called Initial Impressions a week or so after you had gotten to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's MM/2. And in it -- I don't think we have to put it up on the board. This is very informal and I'll just read it to you. And you said: "The next RC," that's regional centre, right, "is due to open tomorrow, Pec, but I can't help feeling that Canada did not get much mileage from having been given the opportunity of taking command of the first," you have first underlined, "first one to open here in Prizren. So far I have given three interviews all to foreign journalists and I have not seen any press release or media advisory. Is there any play in the Canadian media?" Now, isn't this just a very understandable pride that you'd like folks to know that Canada is -- you know, that's the country that opened the first regional centre in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And very absolutely understandable. And I take it understandable that Colonel Delic expressed the emotions that he felt about his country?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And whereas you can, as an outsider coming in, can just call them the -- what was the word you used? You don't want to use the word terrorists. What was the word you were using?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Guerillas or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What was it? Liberation -- freedom fighters, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Freedom fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you understand that the emotional depth of the Serb -- I mean, to a Serb they are indeed terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I tried to understand the emotional attachment of all parties to the land, both the Serbs and the Albanians. And in fact I tried not to make a ruling on that as to who was right in the whole thing. I believe, in fact, both are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in fact, we had a witness. Do you know John Crosland, Colonal Crosland?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't know the name. He said in his opinion -- he was a military attache to the British Embassy, and he said as far as -- taking Kosovo out of Serbia is like taking Wales out of England. So -- you're nodding your head. So I'm just trying -- do you understand the depth of the attachment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, again you were in Kosovo and the Pristina -- Prizren area for about three months. And it's fair to say, is it not, that there was a strong KLA presence in your area as well as other areas of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that under the October 25th, 1998, Clark-Naumann Agreement, and with Mr. Milosevic, VJ and MUP forces were required to decrease their forces in Kosovo to the levels preceding the outbreak of terrorist activities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And again, to save time here, because we have a few people coming after me to ask you some questions, I take it that you would agree with the words of General Naumann, who was the chairman of the NATO military committee, and I'll read you exactly what he had to say about this and he's testified to that effect at this trial several weeks ago. He said: "I think it's fair to say that Milosevic honoured the commitment which he had made to General Clark and myself on 25 October 1998. He withdrew the forces and he withdrew the police. There may have been some difference as to whether there were 200 or 400 policemen more or less, but that really does not matter. More or less, he honoured the commitment. Then the UCK or KLA filled the void the withdrawn forces had left, and they escalated. I have stated this in the NATO Council in October and November repeatedly. In most cases the escalation came from the Kosovar side, not from the Serb side." Do you agree with what General Naumann had to say here, General Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I would say that during my time there I did not see any increase in either of the Serb or the KLA presence, except towards the end of my time, before I actually left on leave in March, where there seemed to be an increase in, I would say, recruiting by the Albanian side of individuals and so on. But I think the levels up to that time were pretty even, both the Serb and the KLA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I will try for the next 15 or 20 minutes or so to show you very respectfully that you might be mistaken, because I'm going to show you a series of KVM reports which indicate to the contrary, but again I respect your opinion.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And about the same time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please, counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Toward the end of December 1998 -- in fact, in November of 1998, a gentlemen named Bislim Zyrapi -- do you know who he is, by the way?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Bislim Zyrapi became the Chief of Staff of the KLA General Staff in November of 1998. And he actually testified here several weeks ago. And he said, and this is Prosecution Exhibit 2460, and he's speaking now as of December 28th, 1998, this is a report that he was giving to his zone commanders. He said: "Following the enemy offensive, the re-positioning of forces has been carried out in all the OZs," operating zones, "and we can freely say that the territory controlled by our units is now of a greater percentage than prior to the enemy offensive." Do you feel there's some truth to that from what you know of the situation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: As I say, for me -- I would say that it was certainly transparent. I was not looking at, you know, how much territory was being held by the KLA at what time. I was looking for the ability to have freedom of movement throughout both the KLA and the Serb areas, for example, the border. So I can't give you a judgement as to whether more areas were being held or not. First of all, I arrived on the 15th of -- you know, in Prizren by the 15th of December, so by the 28th of December I could not give you one way or the other whether that was the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go on now and show other occupation of territory and provocations, and this is all partially, too, to gauge -- for the Trial Chamber to gauge your comment about Serb forces overreacting, because I'm trying to show what they were reacting against.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And so a specific instance is the Podujevo situation in late December 1998. Do you remember that as sort of a troubled area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yeah. I'd have to see a map again and look at my notes, but I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's up there in northern-eastern Kosovo. It's in between Serbia. It's sort of a main road --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the Podujevo situation, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the KVM -- there's an interim report period covered 21 to 27 December 1998, a KVM report. And it says: "The VJ withdrew from positions in this area in accordance with the agreement, but then watched as those positions were occupied and fortified by the KLA. The area is of particular strategic importance to the Serbs, since the main north-south highway from Belgrade is within it. But the same pattern of KLA occupying areas left by the security forces has been observed elsewhere in Kosovo." So does that get you back into the situation now? Is that beginning to sound very familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Except that, of course, Podujevo was outside of my personal area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right, but I take it you did try to keep abreast of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: To some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In fact, I think you even took General DZ's place for a week?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When he went on vacation or something you took his place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And on the next page of this report it says: "Measuring KLA defiance is more problematic since it is not a partner to any agreement; however, the reported decision of the KLA to end the unilateral cease-fire it declared in October would be implemented -- it would, if implemented, be a clear contradiction of Resolution 1199, which emphasises that all elements in the Kosovo Albanian community should pursue their goals by peaceful means only. The KLA claims its modified stance results from the attacks of Serb security forces; however, the KLA may see it in their interest to provoke Serb reactions that would increase the chances of NATO military intervention in Kosovo." And my question to you, General: Isn't that more or less what happened over the next few months to the beginning of the war, repeated KLA provocations and reactions to those provocations by Serb forces. Isn't that what happened, more or less?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: In certain instances -- certainly in my area we really tried to keep the lid on these kinds of provocations to try and -- to ensure that the status quo would remain to allow the political situation to be sorted out, but I certainly couldn't take issue with this report from the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And one incident, unfortunately, that you couldn't keep the lid on was an ambush in -- on January 8th, 1999, where a press release issued by OSCE says: "The KLA executed a meticulously planned ambush of a column of MUP vehicles, leading to three deaths and several casualties. These actions are in direct contradiction of solemn promises from the KLA of showing restraint and of maintaining the cease-fire agreement. KVM wishes to make it clear that it finds the reaction by Yugoslavian authorities to these KLA provocations has been up to this point very restrained. The representatives of the Yugoslavian authorities have shone a willingness to cooperate in the present situation." And you probably remember that incident quite well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I do. Matter of fact, the reason why this press release was issued is because I pressed for it. I wanted it to be issued to show that there had been, certainly, a good -- a restrained response and that the KLA were violating the agreement in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And of course you were in Prizren, but there was an assessment for 8 January 1999 and that's P407, Prosecution Exhibit 407, at page 158 where the KVM assessment is: "The KLA appears to be taking advantage of OSCE's presence and becoming more provocative in their actions." Again, I'm trying to get to the point now of it was the KLA that was becoming more and more provocative, not Serb forces. That's why I'm asking you these questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess I would accept that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This isn't supposed to be a speech by Mr. Sepenuk. We're looking for your answers on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would accept -- certainly in the case of Podujevo and also in the case of the ambush, it was definitely a provocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's making a much more general point that between your arrival and the start of the war, the true picture was increasing provocation by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it would be difficult for me to be categoric and say that there was an increase as time went on. But obviously as you look at these -- some of these points that are being brought up here, some of these reports as a matter of fact, it points to that. I could not argue with that, you know, the written word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we're not here to hear your -- just -- no criticism of you. But we're not here to hear your analysis of a series of documents; we're here to hear your experience. And if you've no experience, I'd like you to say it, because I don't want this to go on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's it, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- on the basis that you're going to give the nod to what he says without knowing anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is my point, Your Honour, is that from my point of view, we really tried to keep the lid on things both -- on both sides and in terms of provocation, you know, you could link all these things together but for me the individual incidents that I dealt with when I was on the ground there did not show me that there was a great increase in provocation from either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, that's why I'm asking these question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I will attempt to -- I maintain my thesis but we'll see as we go along. There's an assessment, a KVM assessment for 8 January 1999, Prosecution Exhibit 407, page 156, and it again speaks about that ambush that we just talked about. And it says: "It appears the KLA does not acknowledge the cease-fire any more and will most likely strike again using the same tactics." And it goes on to say: "The subsequent assault by the KLA on this check-point indicates the KLA's high level of confidence and willing to attack in multiple locations." Now, I want to move from there to a meeting I don't think you had, sir. I think that you were not at this meeting but you've initialled the record that we have. It's one of the attachments to your statement. Mr. -- Colonel Morwood was there.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Cobb-Smith, one of the liaisons, Mr. Lefever, one of the liaisons, and Drini from the KLA. And it's a meeting record with the KLA 23 January 1999, and your initials appear at the bottom, and I had a great deal of difficulty trying to figure out what number this document was. Maybe Mr. Marcussen can help. It's virtually unreadable at the top of the document, but it's K0075720. And just for the sake of the record, if Mr. Marcussen can simply give me what the number is, I'd appreciate it. And while -- maybe I should wait. Well, let me read from it. I don't think there's any doubt as to what it says, and maybe at the break Mr. Marcussen and I can find the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he's going to help you, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's part of attachment MM/14A --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- which has three documents and it's the last one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in this document it says -- and this is supposedly what Drini told your associates and your colleagues. "KLA" -- 23 January, 1999. "KLA's plan for a more general resumption of hostilities were complete, while they, the KLA, might not be fighting now, this was their choice, they would choose the most suitable time and place for future action. Sufficient latitude was available now to zone commanders to initiate limited attacks as they saw fit." And then later on in the statement it says: "Taking the campaign to the towns was an active element in the next military steps of the KLA." And I take it that that was a report furnished to you by your colleagues, and was there any particular reaction on your part to what appeared to be Drini's plan for the future?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And in the context of that -- of that meeting this was, of course, after Racak and Drini -- certainly there was -- I felt there was a certain amount of bluster in there about, you know, we're prepared to go and the reason we're not going is because we choose not to do it at this time. But there's no question that everyone was watching what was going on. There's the issue of we're in the middle of winter as well, so perhaps the weather had an influence on what they wanted to do. But as I say, our aim was to say, Fine, don't attack. Try to keep things reasonably steady for the moment and let the political process carry on. And certainly when Rambouillet negotiations began, we really tried to keep the lid on it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I can go on, Your Honour -- excuse me. Strike what I just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, strike what I just said. I was thinking of another break at another time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The -- you were saying you were trying to keep the lid on, but it didn't quite happen that way, because the next document we have here is 3D374 and this is an assessment for 14 February 1999, which is, you know, a few weeks after that January 23rd meeting with Drini. And it says: "Even with the conduct of small-scale military and terrorist actions in the past several days, Kosovo has remained relatively quiet. The reason for this is probably due to the meeting in Rambouillet, each side wanting to be seen as favouring peace in the region. On the same token, some of these incidents can be viewed as acts of provocation," and it says here "mainly by the KLA, trying to provoke reactionary oppositions by the other which can then be exploited in the international arena." So again, a KVM assessment that the acts of provocation were mainly by the KLA. And you of course know and worked with General DZ; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, it's P2508, he said in paragraph 189 about this period, he says: "I must say that during the Rambouillet discussions the number of incidents instigated by the Serbs declined significantly, whereas those instigated by the KLA declined much less appreciably. Furthermore, the KLA became more opportunistic during this time." Does that what General DZ said square with your memory now of what went on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It certainly does, and that's what I mentioned is that towards the end of my period there, there was a greater, you know, amount of recruitment and kind of a -- I guess I would say -- we assessed it at the time -- I assessed it at the time as a kind of positioning themselves by the KLA for what the future might bring in terms of an accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then by way of another KVM document, the scale of violence initiated by the KLA rose drastically during the period 23 February to 11 March 1999. And this document, a KVM document, says: "Unprovoked attacks by the KLA against the police have continued and the number of casualties sustained by the security forces has increased." And then if you go inside the document there's a whole series, and I'm simply not going to go over -- I don't think I should because there's simply not time. But there's a whole series of provocations by the KLA. I will give a few of them if you don't mind. It says first of all on 27 February a police patrol was ambushed west of Pristina airfield with one police officer killed and one wounded, apparently by KLA sniper fire. And then it says: "There's a new area of military engagement," and it goes on to talk about reports of fighting near Kacanik in south-western Kosovo and one police officer, the commander of the Kacanik police station was killed, four policemen wounded, an estimated 2.000 people fled villages in the Kacanik area, some trying to cross the border to Macedonia. And the thought here, at least I'm going to express a thought here and see if you agree with it, that the KLA was attempting to provide access for a possible NATO ground invasion through Macedonia. And during any of your three months as head of the Pristina region -- Prizren region, excuse me, General, was that ever in your -- on your radar screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: The incidents you talk about, for example, Kacanik and so on, definitely I was aware that this was going on, and in fact I believe that this -- the rising in activity by the KLA and the response by the Serb forces and the increased fighting in that area is what resulted in the mission being evacuated. So I was aware that that was the case, but again certainly in my area I don't remember -- I don't remember any activities that we could have assessed as being preparing the ground for a NATO invasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know a gentleman by the name Christopher John Clark, does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He's a warrant officer --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- with 16 years the British army, paratrooper, commando, combat, mountain leader -- he's got all sorts of credentials. And he was the operations officer in Kosovo. And he says, by the way -- I'll just simply ask your opinion. I'm going to guess you're going to disagree with him. He says: "As time went on I became involved with liaison with the KLA, this was due to the fact that the KLA was responsible in most cases," maybe you won't disagree, "was responsible in most cases for breaking the Holbrooke Agreement." Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Not in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Not in your area despite what we've just been hearing, right? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by that last reference, Mr. Sepenuk, in spite of what we've been hearing? Is Kacanik in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, so what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I was referring to overall, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's increasingly sounding like a closing argument, Mr. Sepenuk, because it's clear that you're asking the witness about things of which he's got little direct personal knowledge, and it would be helpful, I think, while we've got his valuable time to concentrate on what he can actually deal with personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll go to one of the last documents I have and that is the document actually authored by David Wilson. I take it it's the same David Wilson who is -- who is he, who was David Wilson?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: David Wilson was an officer from the British army who was working with the UK KDOM before I arrived in Kosovo. And therefore, when I deployed in Prizren and we -- the KVM took over the UK KDOM or absorbed the UK KDOM he became one of my officers, and I employed him as intelligence fusion centre and kind of a future -- he turned out to be an officer who had good knowledge of the ground, of the parties' good kind of political background and one who could think laterally. So I used him a lot to put assessments together, and although they were his own, some of them I thought were pretty accurate, certainly food for thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you think he's a fairly astute person?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I think he's an astute person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in this exhibit, this is Prosecution Exhibit 641, I believe, yes, he has -- and we've been moving through February, March --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And by the way, Your Honour, I'll just say for the record there were a lot of incidents in this last report 3D179 and I respectfully comment to the Court there are a number of incidents of KLA provocations in this, Your Honour, and just I direct it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Sepenuk. All of these are available for us to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he says -- this is his assessment of KLA attitudes and we're about a week away from the war now in March 15th -- and this is the last document I'll talk to you about. And he says that: "Prior to the first round of peace talks at Rambouillet the KLA presented an apparently unified and disciplined front. Their lines of command and control from the General Staff to the zone commanders and below seemed to be generally effective." That's his assessment. And then he talks about recent events, and again I'll just very briefly summarise them. There's a number of events that he talks about which show KLA provocation like in Kacanik he says that: "During the build-up of this operation in the Kacanik area, the KLA brigade commander in the area refused to let the UNHCR evacuate IDPs from the area. This has been seen as a cynical attempt to use Albanian civilians as a human shield." I take it you knew nothing about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And there's several other matters mentioned, the Dulje Heights ambush, Lebane shooting, and one I will mention, that is the kidnapped Albanian police employee. It says: "The KLA General Staff have admitted that the Albanian police employee was arrested by the KLA secret service for being a spy and that he's being held at their information centre. This is the first time that the KLA have admitted to having a region-wide police unit that conducts this type of operation. Again, the General Staff were not willing to acknowledge that this return to terrorist kidnappings was not to their benefit." Now, the whole notion of the abduction and the murder of Albanians, I was a bit disturbed, again I say very respectfully, by your testimony in the Milosevic case where you didn't seem to know about it. Do you know about it now? Do you know that there were many abductions of ethnic Albanians because they had -- did business with the Serbs or because the Serbs [sic] considered them as collaborators?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I didn't have any direct knowledge at the time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please make significantly longer pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear your answer because the interpreter says that we're stepping over each other's lines. I'm sure I'm the prime offender.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I didn't have direct knowledge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The interpreter was speaking. I'm sorry. Can you give your answer once more, please. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Okay. I had no knowledge at the time or little knowledge at the time, and since then of course I've come to understand that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And my last question on this document pretty much -- my next-to-last question for you is it says in this document: "If the Serbian government refuses to sign the agreement, the KLA local commanders," and he's talking about a peace agreement now, "will consider the political effort to have been a failure and will return to full-scale violence to fight for independence. Many of the KLA at the zone command level and below are under the misapprehension that the KLA can defeat the Serbian security forces. If this happens, certain parts of the KLA, for example Ramush," and he's referring there obviously to Ramush Haradinaj, correct? It has to be for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. "Will probably attempt to take the fight into the towns and cities." And of course as we know. There was no peace agreement and the war started about a week later.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And my last question for you, General, is that memo that the same David Wilson, who I think you consider a fairly astute guy prepared. It's attached to your statement and I ask you about it only because in your statement you said you think it's an accurate assessment of the Kosovo situation --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Generally accurate, generally accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I hesitate to use it, because it's one man's opinion and, you know, he could be right he could be wrong, but I'm going to ask you about one small part, and this gets back to the simple soldier, if I might, and here's what he says. He says, talking about the VJ, he says: "The key group obviously are the professional officers" talking about again the army, the VJ, and the SNCOs, the non-commissioned officers --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Senior NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. "From their point of view they are frustrated, contemptuous of the political manoeuvrings, angered at the double humiliation of being scrutinised -- the word 'scrutinised' is in quotes -- by foreign observers in their own land and being required to observe a cease-fire against terrorists and skeptical -- skeptical about the prospects of a political settlement while the analogies with western forces can easily be overdone, it is comparatively easy for any soldier to understand their emotions." Now, David Wilson was a soldier, was he not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And obviously, sir, you're a very high-ranking and distinguished soldier. Do you think there's truth to what he has to say?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think it accurately reflects the feelings from Colonel Delic on down to probably soldiers on the ground of the VJ forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which document is that, Mr. Sepenuk, is that MM/15?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't mention it for the record. I apologise for that. It's MM/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: MM/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maisonneuve, my name is Djuro Cepic and I'm one of the Defence counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic and I have several questions for you. I will start from your arrival in Prizren. In your statement in paragraph 13 you state that you arrived on the 15th of December, 1998, there and immediately you were involved in the border skirmishes involving the death of 35 men who were allegedly members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Later on you were able to confirm that these were indeed members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, for the majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that all those who were killed, wounded, and captured in that action on the other side were, indeed, members of the KLA and that your verifiers, including Jan [as interpreted] Henry and other members of your regional centre, were able to see that for themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that the majority were KLA. There may have been one or two accompanying people there but the majority were KLA, we certainly thought that they were KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you clarify the name of the verifier referred to there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jan Henry I think he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That name's familiar to you, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Iain Henry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Iain Henry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe later on you learned that this group of the total of 150 KLA soldiers went across the border from Albania into the territory of the FRY and that several KLA members were arrested and a sizeable amount of weapons were confiscated, and these were the latest type of weaponry, as well as a considerable amount of money?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't remember actually hearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Maisonneuve. Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I was just going to ask for a reference to what it is my learned colleague is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When this sort of situation arises, it would be helpful if you delayed your request for that until the witness answers rather than interrupt the flow. But can you assist, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I even have several video-clips that can confirm the statements I've been putting to the witness. In addition to that, in e-court we have in the document 3470 which is Iain Henry's statement. With your leave, I would like for the first video-clip to be played, which shows the presence of the verifiers on the spot as well as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. What do you know of this incident, Mr. Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I arrived, as correctly stated, on the 15th of December and essentially I was brand new to the place and I had arrived and I heard there was of course this -- there was this engagement. And at that point my main task, as I saw it, was to ensure the ordinarily transition of the bodies from one party to the other. And so that's basically what I remember of the event. It was a -- kind of a shocking way to arrive in theatre, but I don't remember in fact seeing Mr. Henry's specific report and I don't remember hearing about a quantity of equipment, et cetera, or weapons that had been brought over at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic, it doesn't look as though the witness can help in any meaningful way on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the broadcasting of the video-clip, which speaks of the amount of weapons confiscated, might serve to refresh the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you think that, then I can't argue with you at the moment. Let's see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could Defence Exhibit 5D116 be played, please. It's very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maisonneuve, were you present at this place where weapons were exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I was not. No, I was not, but the infamous David Wilson is the person that you see on there, so if you're wondering what he looked like, that was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You got lucky there, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have a lot of material that could point in that direction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But let us briefly go back to the situation we mentioned. I suppose your verifiers told you that the army behaved very professionally and humanely, both toward those who were captured and toward the bodies of dead KLA members. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You are aware that on that occasion they allowed your verifiers to speak to the captured KLA members, among whom there were even some women?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I believe I do remember that. Certainly in the transfer of the bodies, and there was total cooperation by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maisonneuve. The conclusion is, therefore, that the army in this incident as well as in all the other incidents in the border area between the FRY and Albania conducted themselves in a professional fashion and humanely. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think this calls for complete speculation and cannot be answered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree. The witness can answer the question to the extent that he has experience of the conduct of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my experience, Your Honour, yes, the VJ conducted themselves professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 549th Brigade, headed by Colonel Delic, also did not use heavy weaponry. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already mentioned him today. Let us mention him for the third time in the past 15 minutes and that's Mr. David Wilson and his document MM/4. According to what your verifiers were able to see, the VJ when discussing the period that Mr. Wilson discussed, the VJ behaved professionally, did not go into the villages, and were successful in their action in the border area. This is item 8D of MM/4, wherein Wilson's observation is contained. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That would be an accurate description, I believe, for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maisonneuve. Today the Prosecutor also referred to MM/2B. Just give me a moment to find the document in this binder. This is the document concerning the implementation of liaison measures in response to an agreement on the future status of Kosovo dated the 23rd of February, 1999. This document, among other issues, mentions that within your area of responsibility, that's to say of the regional centre of the Kosovo Verification Mission, 121st, 122nd, and 124th Brigades were present in Orahovac and 123rd Brigade in Suva Reka. The commander of the entire area was Mr. Drini, whom you mentioned in several of your notes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And everything that I have just said is consistent with what you reported on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] In addition to the four brigades we mentioned, do you know whether there was any other brigade operational within the area of your responsibility in -- for the duration of your stay in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Not specifically. As a matter of fact, I did not deal with the brigades; I dealt with Drini exclusively. And my coordination centre heads were the ones that discussed and worked with the brigades, at the brigade level, their level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maisonneuve. Let us go back to Mr. David Wilson. Among other things, in item 4 of this document, MM/4, he mentions the existence of village units. I'm interested in hearing about these village units. They were composed of villagers of a given village only who had automatic weaponry, but mostly had no uniforms. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: It perhaps is the case again -- I did not go into the great fine details that he was reporting here, but I certainly trust his judgement that he -- because of his knowledge of the UK -- during UK KDOM period as well as the time that we were with the KVM that I would trust his judgement that he's reporting accurately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maisonneuve. Do you perhaps recall one of the reports given to you by your subordinates in relation to these village units? Were they part of brigades or independent units? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I do not recall, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose you'll remember my next question. In your meetings with Mr. Drini and the reports as a result of these meetings, you said that you met in a house. Were these meetings always held in one village or would they have several venues? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: They moved from village to village, in different villages, depending on where Drini was at the time, and they usually took place at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These meeting houses were, in fact, KLA HQs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I believe some of them were. I believe some of them were houses where they might have meetings themselves, but I'm not -- you know, I cannot say that they had a headquarters in certain places.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps observe on some of your visits that in the other houses there were KLA members billeted, that they did not have classic-type camp facilities, but that they used private homes as their billeting facilities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I could not say that I observed specific instances of that, but I think that would accurately describe the times that I went to visit Drini to -- that I went to speak to him, that would accurately describe the kind of approach that the KLA had. They were in the villages and housed in the houses in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These villages were their bases?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement paragraph 53, you state when describing the incident which took place on the 8th of January involving the murder of three police officers, that there were well-fortified trenches from which the police came under attack. I will play a brief video-clip now and will ask you a question at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Defence Exhibit 5D117 played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not interested in the sound. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson [sic], in this video-clip we can see trenches in the villages. I suppose that very often when you came into the villages where there were KLA present, you would see trenches on the approach roads to the villages?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you see them next to the houses where there were KLA members present or did you also observe them next to homes that were populated by residents?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I can't say I ever saw trenches in the villages. Just let me think for a moment. I think I -- I think I saw some trenches on an incident of -- in an area very close to Prizren who -- in a small village whose name escapes me now fairly close to the end of my time in the area. But otherwise I don't remember that as a standard procedure that was being used in the villages that I visited. And I'd just like to ask you a question about this video. What was this video supposed to be of? Was this the video that was supposed to be of the incident of the 8th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just the trenches in villages. The trenches you mentioned, where were they located precisely, if you can remember? Were they within the village or outside the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you can recall.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I think they were on the edge of the village in this particular case, and it was like one were two trenches for one or two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've gone through your transcript carefully. Did you perhaps receive from your associates some sort of an estimation or perhaps do you have an estimation as to the numbers of KLA soldiers who were within the area of responsibility of regional centre 1?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't recall a number being given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maisonneuve. Let us briefly go back to Mr. Wilson and his document that's been referred to several times here. You will also agree with all the other observations he made or assessments he made, namely that the KLA achieved great success between March and July of 1998. My question for you is: Can you roughly in terms of percentages tell us the size of the area held by KLA members in the vicinity of your regional centre?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: That would be -- it would be very difficult for me to estimate unless I had a map and was able to point it out. But even that -- it was not -- it was not, I don't think, an absolute area. There were certain areas where we tried to come -- to go on patrol but they would not let us. They were also impeding our freedom of movement, there's no question, and so they would not let us go into areas, but I would have difficulty kind of pinning it to a certain number of kilometres or square kilometres. I think that information's available, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now that we are -- that we've mentioned the freedom of movement, let me mention this one matter. This is MM/14A dated the 4th of March, 1999, where in paragraph 4 Drini says: "I ordered that a curfew be introduced for civilians in our areas for their own safety." You wouldn't be able to tell us, even in rough terms, to which area this curfew may have applied?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, but I would estimate that if Drini was speaking -- when I spoke to Drini I understood that he was talking about his operational zone. So I would imagine that it was within his -- the boundaries of his operational zone, which I think were fairly close to the boundaries of the Prizren province or areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was operations zone Pastrik on the part of the KLA. Do you know that the KLA had in that area and in the area of Dukagjin special units for rapid action and liquidation of kidnapped persons? Were you aware of the existence of these units at the time of your stay there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maisonneuve, you stand by the statement that you said in Milosevic case on page 5817 that the KLA is a rebellious organisation consisting of paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE
utterances.text: Yes, I think I -- that's -- I was trying to describe what kind of force I perceived them as, and I think that's as accurate as you can be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, is it the proper time for stopping?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How much more cross do you have, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Roughly 45 minutes or half an hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all good things must come to an end every day, so I'm afraid we've run out of time and we have to abandon today's sitting at this stage. However, you will require to return tomorrow. It's important that you don't have any discussion with anybody overnight about your evidence at that -- and that means either the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give in the case. Whoever you talk to and whatever you talk about, make sure it's not the evidence. And if you leave with the usher, we'll see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
